Commissioner.

On the afternoon of August 6, Mr Ivanov called on me at Broadway Mansions and reported that he received a threatening telephone call at his residence from some unknown person. The caller asked for Mr. Ivanov and when the latter answered the telephone he was asked: "Is it true you are going to take over the post of Chairman of the Russian Emigrants' Committee?" Mr Ivanov replied would but the matter had not been decided finally. In answer to this the caller said: "Take our advice and do not that. It is very risky and you may follow Kutzler." Mr Ivanov enquired who was speaking and all he got was "Never mind, but only take our advice." The voice was threatening and the conversation was in English. Mr Ivanov described the voice as high and though that it might have been that of a Chinese although the English was very good and without accent. He was positive it was not a Japanese.

Mr. Ivanov's office and residence are located at Brooklyn Court, 175 L Route des Soeurs, Apt. 53 (telephone 79849). He has made similar report to the French Police. I pointed out that if he desired any special protection he should consult the French Police and the S.M. Police would co-operate if necessary. Mr Ivanov then referred to an untrue report of the arrest of General Kupoff, which appeared in the Evening Post. He had placed the matter of this libel in the hands of Mr. Allman who, however, considered that a correction and apology by the paper would suffice.

Mr Ivanov next said he felt it a duty to the Russian community that he take over the post vacated by Mr. Kutzler and when asked who was the prime mover in offering him post he named Suzuki San (Far Eastern Times) who had arranged him an interview with the Chief of Police, Lu Ying, and Mayor Fu Hsiao-an, the latter promising the fullest protection in Chinese territory, International Settlement and French Concession. I suggested that it might have been better if his appointment had not been made so hurriedly and Mr. Ivanov said he was of the same opinion and had suggested to Suzuki San, a postponement permitting the Kutzler tragedy to die down a bit, but the latter wanted things done with all speed. Mr Ivanov here remarked that he did not particularly want this job which was keenly sought by General Gleboff, the nominee of the Japanese Naval Landing Party.

D.O. (Grime)

日期：1942年8月18日

警务总监。

8月6日下午，伊万诺夫先生（Mr Ivanov）在百老汇大厦拜访了我，并报告称他在家中接到一个不明身份者的威胁电话。来电者要找伊万诺夫先生，当后者接听电话时，对方问道：“你真的要接任俄国侨民委员会主席一职吗？”伊万诺夫先生回答说有此意向，但此事尚未最终决定。对此，来电者说：“听我们的劝告，不要那样做。这非常危险，你可能会步库茨勒（Kutzler）的后尘。”伊万诺夫先生询问对方是谁，得到的回答只是：“别管是谁，只听我们的劝告。”声音带有威胁性，谈话使用英语。伊万诺夫先生形容该声音尖细，认为可能是中国人，尽管其英语非常好且没有口音。他确信不是日本人。

伊万诺夫先生的办公室和住所位于姐妹路（Route des Soeurs）175号布鲁克林公寓（Brooklyn Court）53室（电话79849）。他已向法租界巡捕房作了类似报告。我指出，如果他需要任何特别保护，应咨询法租界巡捕房，如有必要，工部局警务处将予以配合。随后，伊万诺夫先生提到《晚邮报》（Evening Post）刊登的一则关于库波夫将军（General Kupoff）被捕的不实报道。他将这起诽谤事件交由奥尔曼先生（Mr. Allman）处理，但奥尔曼先生认为，由报社进行更正并道歉就足够了。

伊万诺夫先生接着表示，他觉得接替库茨勒先生留下的空缺职位是对俄国侨民社区应尽的义务。当被问及是谁主要推动向他提供这一职位时，他提到了铃木先生（Suzuki San，《远东时报》），此人安排他会见了警察局长卢英和市长傅筱庵，后者承诺在华界、公共租界和法租界提供全面保护。我建议，如果他的任命不那么仓促可能会更好，伊万诺夫先生表示同意，并曾向铃木先生建议推迟任命，让库茨勒悲剧的影响稍加平息，但后者希望尽快行事。伊万诺夫先生在此评论说，他并不特别想要这份工作，而日本海军陆战队提名的格列博夫将军（General Gleboff）却极力谋求此职。

行动主管（格里姆）

Subject Interview with Mr. N.A. Ivanoff.

Made by D.S.I. Prokofiev. Forwarded by Supt. J. Mason.

At 11 a.m. on 4-8-40 Mr. N.A. Ivanoff, Russian
Attorney and Counsellor-at-Law with office at 153 -L
Route des Soeurs, Apt. 53 ( Brooklyn Court ), residing at
the same address, called at the Special Branch and request-
ed an interview. He was interviewed by P.A. to D.C. (Spe-
cial Branch) and the undersigned.

During the course of the interview he stated
that the object of his visit was to find out, in strictest
confidence, the opinion of the Police regarding the motives
for the assassination of Mr. Ch.E. Metzler and the party
responsible for the crime or, to be more exact, if there is
any evidence to show that the party sponsoring the forma-
tion of the "Association of Russian Emigrants in Shanghai",
409 East Seward Road, as announced in the newspaper "Rus"
on 1-6-40, is in any way connected with or otherwise res-
ponsible for the crime. It is of the utmost importance to
him, Mr. Ivanoff continued, to know this in order that he
could make up his mind as to whether or not he should ac-
cept the offer of the Japanese authorities to appoint him
head of the new representative body for the Russian com-
munity in Shanghai.

Referring to the well known attempt of General
V.D. Kosmin's group ( sponsored by Captain K.Kuroki, a
representative of the Japanese military authorities ) to
dislodge the Russian Emigrants Committee, Mr. Ivanoff went
on to say that some time towards the end of June, 1940,
when the failure of the attempt in question seemed appa-
rent, a certain Russian named V.I. Karpoff, who styles him-

主题 与 N.A. 伊万诺夫先生的会谈。

由副督察普罗科菲耶夫（Prokofiev）制作。由警司 J. 梅森（J. Mason）转呈。

1940年8月4日上午11时，N.A. 伊万诺夫先生，俄国律师及法律顾问，办公室位于姐妹路（Route des Soeurs）153号布鲁克林公寓53室，居住地址相同，到访政治部并要求会见。他由政治部助理副总监及下文签署人进行了接见。

在会谈过程中，他表示此次来访的目的是为了在最严格保密的情况下，了解警方对查·埃·梅茨勒先生（Ch.E. Metzler）遇刺动机及负责该罪行的派系的看法，或者更确切地说，是否有任何证据表明，正如1940年6月1日《罗斯报》（Rus）所宣布的那样，赞助成立“上海俄国侨民协会”（东熙华德路409号）的派系与该罪行有任何关联或需为此负责。伊万诺夫先生继续说，对他而言，知晓这一点至关重要，以便他能决定是否接受日本当局任命他为上海俄国侨民社区新代表机构负责人的提议。

谈到众所周知的弗·德·科斯明将军（General V.D. Kosmin）集团（由日本军方代表黑木大尉（Captain K.Kuroki）赞助）试图推翻俄国侨民委员会一事，伊万诺夫先生接着说，在1940年6月底左右，当上述企图显然失败时，一位自称将军及日本宪兵队总部顾问的俄国人 V.I. 卡尔波夫（V.I. Karpoff）到他家中拜访，并与他就梅茨勒先生进行了交谈。卡尔波夫特别提到，梅茨勒先生是一名共济会成员，他在俄国侨民委员会中的同伙中有许多其他共济会成员和苏联特工，梅茨勒先生的态度是反俄的，其活动旨在瓦解俄国侨民社区。卡尔波夫甚至断言，在宣布成立“俄国侨民协会”之后，梅茨勒先生受当地共济会命令不惜一切手段反对该计划，并为此获得了10万美元用于宣传。最后，卡尔波夫建议伊万诺夫先生会见一位名叫池田（Ikeda）的日本人，他将其描述为一位关心上海俄国侨民事务的俄语翻译。伊万诺夫先生同意会见此人。这导致伊万诺夫、池田、黑木、卡尔波夫和科斯明将军之间在伊万诺夫先生住所进行了一系列会谈。日本人及其俄国同伴对俄国侨民公共生活的历史表现出浓厚的兴趣。伊万诺夫先生是上海的老居民，前俄国副领事及领事法官，他满足了访客的好奇心，并向他们提供了大量关于该主题的文档资料。结果，他们得出结论，应该是伊万——

Inter alia, Karpoff mentioned that Mr. Metzler was a freemason, that there were many other freemasons and Soviet agents amongst his associates in the Russian Emigrants Committee, that Mr. Metzler's attitude was anti-Russian and his activities were directed towards disintegration of the Russian emigrant community. Karpoff even went as far as to assert that following the announcement regarding the formation of the "Association of Russian Emigrants" Mr. Metzler was ordered by local freemasons to oppose the scheme by every means and was given by them $100.000 for propaganda purposes in this connection. In conclusion Karpoff suggested that Mr. Ivanoff should meet a certain Japanese named Ikeda, whom he described as a Russian interpreter interested in the affairs of the Russian community in Shanghai. Mr. Ivanoff agreed to meet the latter individual. This resulted in a series of interviews between Messrs Ivanoff, Ikeda, Kuroki, Karpoff and General Kosmin which took place at Mr. Ivanoff's residence. The Japanese and their Russian associates displayed a vivid interest in the history of the public life of the Russian community. Mr. Ivanoff, an old resident of Shanghai, former Russian Vice-Consul and Consular Judge, satisfied the curiosity of his visitors and put at their disposal extensive documental data on the subject in question. As a result, they came to the conclusion that it was Mr. Iva-

诺夫先生而不是梅茨勒先生应该成为已故的弗·弗·格罗塞先生（Mr. V.F. Grosse）在俄国侨民委员会主席职位上的继任者，因为他的资历仅次于格罗塞先生。最后，黑木大尉建议任命伊万诺夫先生为上海俄国侨民社区重组后的代表机构负责人。

伊万诺夫先生在原则上表示同意，但提出了他的财务状况问题。他指出，他的处境与已故的格罗塞先生和梅茨勒先生不同，前者是工部局的带薪顾问，后者有独立的经济来源，而他，伊万诺夫先生，依靠律师执业为生，如果担任俄国侨民社区负责人，将无法同时从事律师工作。他建议自己被任命为新机构的无薪顾问，该职位不会干扰他的专业活动。对此，黑木大尉评论说，这是一个次要问题，日后很容易安排。然而，经过一番斟酌，他同意了伊万诺夫先生的建议。

随后，在黑木大尉的安排下，伊万诺夫先生与日本副总领事松田先生（Mr. Matsuda）进行了会谈。松田先生告知伊万诺夫先生，免除梅茨勒先生俄国侨民委员会主席职务的决定已最终作出，且梅茨勒先生已同意——

提交辞呈。在松田先生看来，伊万诺夫先生作为旧俄国总领事馆的高级官员，是最适合领导重组后的俄国侨民社区代表机构的人选。黑木大尉再次指出，该问题的财务方面很容易安排，例如，任命伊万诺夫先生为工部局和公董局（F.M.C.，此处指法公董局或泛指市政机构，依上下文可能指法租界公董局或笔误，通常S.M.C对应工部局，F.M.C可能指French Municipal Council即法公董局）的俄国事务带薪顾问。然而，伊万诺夫先生坚持认为，目前他担任重组机构的无薪顾问更为方便。最后，松田先生和黑木先生同意任命他以这种身份在新机构任职，由津马年科将军（General Tsumanenko）担任主席。这发生在7月25日左右，预计将在8月中旬发布相关公告。

8月2日，梅茨勒先生遇刺后，伊万诺夫拜访了黑木大尉。后者听到消息后显得非常悲痛。他似乎也意识到谣言可能会将他与刺杀案联系起来，并表示他准备发誓与此事毫无关系。在那次场合，黑木大尉坚持要求伊万诺夫先生立即同意担任重组机构的负责人，即使是临时任命。他说他会与傅筱庵市长安排发布为此目的的命令。伊万诺夫先生表示了同意。

to tender his resignation. In the opinion of Mr. Matsuda Mr. Ivanoff,senior official of the old Russian Consulate-General,was the most suitable person to be put at the head of the reorganized representative organ for the Russian community. Captain Kuroki again pointed out that the financial side of the question could be easily arranged,for instance, by appointing Mr. Ivanoff a paid advisor on Russian affairs to both the S.M.C. and F.M.C. However, Mr. Ivanoff maintained that for the time being it would be more convenient for him to act as an advisor to the reorganized body,without pay. Finally, Messrs Matsuda and Kuroki agreed to appoint him to serve in this capacity on the new body,with General Tsumanenko as Chairman. This was on or about July 25,and an announcement to this effect was to be made by the middle of August.
On August 2, after the assassination of Mr. Metzler, Ivanoff visited Captain Kuroki. The latter appeared to be greatly distressed by the news. He also seemed to realise that rumours may connect him with the assassination and stated that he was prepared to swear that he had nothing whatever to do with this affair. On that occasion Captain Kuroki insisted that Mr. Ivanoff should give his immediate consent to act as head of the reorganized body,be it even a temporary appointment. He said that he would arrange with Mayor Fu Siao-en for the issuing of an order to that effect. Mr. Ivanoff gave his consent.

During the evening of August 2 a memorial service for the late Mr. Metzler was held at the Russian Cathedral, 55 Rue Paul Henry, after which Bishop John convened a conference at his house situated at the same address. The conference was attended by some 20 persons, mostly members of the advisory body attached to the Russian Emigrants Committee. Bishop John informed those present that the conference was intended to be of a private character and that no resolutions etc. would be passed. Several speeches were delivered which may be described as being anti-Japanese in character. During the course of the meeting several persons closely connected with the late Mr. Metzler were offered the post as his successor as Chairman of the Russian Emigrants Committee, but one after another declined the offer for various reasons. Finally, Bishop John agreed to act as head of the Russian community pending the election of a new Chairman of the Russian Emigrants Committee.

On August 3 Mr. Ivanoff had an interview with Captain Kuroki and informed the latter of what had happened at the conference. He also suggested that the question of his appointment be indefinitely postponed on account of unforeseen circumstances. Captain Kuroki, however, strongly objected to this suggestion saying that the matter had been finally settled and that on August 5 he would take Mr. Ivanoff to the Chief of the Shanghai City Government Police and then to Mayor Fu-Siao-en.

NORTH CHINA DAILY NEWS 11.10.37.
26224

IN THE
RUSSIAN
COLONY

BY STROY

The life of Shanghai's Russian colony is slipping, more or less, back into to its normal channels. It is doing so more quickly, perhaps, than other nationalities, because for Russian women and children there was no evacuation from Shanghai, but, rather, an influx into Shanghai, back to their husbands, fathers and homesteads from various summer resorts on the coast of China. If it were not for the 2,500 Russian refugees from Wayside and Yangtzepoo, Russians could count themselves as having so far escaped pretty lightly from the catastrophe. Refugees from zones of danger were accommodated in the Russian Club and in the premises of the Sokol Sports Club, and in the matter of food they were generously aided by the French authorities. Many of them, however, lost not only their jobs and homes in the areas which were transformed into battlefields, but in many cases were dispossessed of everything they owned, as not a few Russian businesses—mainly provision stores, restaurants, workshops, bars, cabarets, boarding-houses and so on—existed along Broadway and in the Wayside and Yangtzepoo areas.

These misfortunes are being met stoically and with true Christian humility: "God hath given and God hath taken away." To whom can they complain? Where can they go? Who will compensate them for their losses? Our fellow citizens, Russian Christians, no longer have employment. There were among them many families with six or seven children. All of them are now without means of subsistence. They have lost all their goods. Both Wayside and Yangtzepoo areas present the first rumble of ruin. Let us not waste a day but collect alms in the French Concession while opportunities exist for doing so, and let us give this money to the new committee and with it help our fellow citizens.

Paid at increased rates, though they are, of course, daily exposing themselves to great peril.

A New School

In other spheres the life, of the colony is making its bravest attempts to go back to normal. Schools are re-opening, and even a new one—the Pushkin High School—has made its appearance. The building of the school is specially suited to scholastic work, and a excellent staff of teachers, all men of wide experience and high qualifications, has been selected. It may be definitely stated that no Russian middle school in Shanghai has so far had a staff of teachers so distinguished as this one. As regarding the Commercial School of the Russian Orthodox Confraternity, its premises were, as is known, temporarily taken by the Emergency Cholera Hospital. When this occurred, Dr. D. I. Kasakoff, President of the Russian Orthodox Confraternity, notified the teachers that they were released from their duties. Later a re-registration of the staff was announced, and at present people are again being accepted as students.

《字林西报》 1937年10月11日。
26224

俄罗斯
侨民区
内

作者：STROY

上海的俄罗斯侨民区生活或多或少正回归正常轨道。也许比其他国籍的人更快，因为对于俄罗斯妇女和儿童来说，并没有从上海撤离，反而是从中国沿海各个避暑胜地回流到上海，回到她们的丈夫、父亲和家园身边。如果不是因为有2,500名来自韦斯特区（Wayside，音译）和杨树浦的俄罗斯难民，俄罗斯人可以认为自己迄今为止在这场灾难中幸免于难，损失较轻。来自危险区域的难民被安置在俄罗斯俱乐部和索科尔体育俱乐部的场所内，在食物方面得到了法国当局的慷慨援助。然而，许多人不仅失去了在变成战场的地区的工作和家园，而且在许多情况下，他们所有的财产都被剥夺，因为不少俄罗斯企业——主要是食品店、餐馆、作坊、酒吧、歌舞厅、寄宿公寓等——都存在于百老汇路以及韦斯特区和杨树浦地区。

这些不幸正以坚忍和真正的基督教谦卑态度来面对：“上帝赐予，上帝取走。”他们能向谁抱怨？他们能去哪里？谁会补偿他们的损失？我们的同胞，俄罗斯基督徒，不再拥有工作。他们当中有许多家庭有六七个孩子。现在所有人都失去了生计来源。他们失去了所有财物。韦斯特区和杨树浦地区呈现出毁灭的最初迹象。让我们不要浪费一天时间，趁有机会时在法租界募集施舍，并将这笔钱交给新委员会，以此帮助我们的同胞。

尽管报酬有所增加，但他们当然每天都面临着巨大的危险。

一所新学校

在其他领域，侨民区的生活正做出最勇敢的努力以回归正常。学校正在重新开学，甚至一所新学校——普希金中学——也已出现。该校校舍特别适合教学工作，并选拔了一支优秀的教师队伍，所有教师均经验丰富且资历深厚。可以肯定地说，上海迄今为止没有任何一所俄罗斯中学拥有如此杰出的教师队伍。至于俄罗斯东正教兄弟会的商业学校，众所周知，其校舍曾被紧急霍乱医院临时占用。当这种情况发生时，俄罗斯东正教兄弟会主席 D. I. 卡萨科夫博士通知教师们解除职务。后来宣布对教职员工进行重新登记，目前再次招收学生。

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, MONDAY, AUGUST 9, 1937
23566
5002
// 8 37

IN THE
RUSSIAN
COLONY

By STROY

It may seem strange with what rapt attention and even anxiety Russians watch the turn of events in the North. Groups quickly gather in front of the offices of Russian newspapers, crowding around the handwritten posters which boldly set forth latest developments, and eagerly discuss the possibility of this or the other. Such interest to the question—will there be a war or not, is explained not by some Russian national preference of war to peace, but by the fact that in the past fifteen years Shanghai Russians have dug themselves in so well with their own enterprises and concerns that war today threatens not only themselves and their families, but also their businesses, most of which have succeeded through very hard work. That war should break out at this time would be all the more regrettable as it was only in the beginning of this year that the Russian colony felt the passing of the depression in Shanghai and began to breathe more easily.

In the spring of this year many merchants left for Japan, America and Paris for merchandise; many were plunged into a process of renovating and extending their premises—all in order to meet the coming autumn trade, as the Russians say, "with all guns." Others had the simple hope that with the extra money made this year they could rest and gather further energy in a summer resort, but to all this there may now be put a tragic end. The stock of goods carried by stores is usually not large and needs frequent replenishment, and the slightest delay in this at once threatens the concern with many inconveniences. Credit is also very limited, and the money for the summer is borrowed for short terms at high rates of percentage. Russian clientele is quick to scent unfavourable political changes so that even the smallest of irregularities is enough to throw out of order or even put out of condition the efficient but at all times extremely fragile mechanism of emigrant trade and petty-industry.

Russian Traders

Russian merchants trade chiefly in haberdashery and articles of men's or women's dress. Then, in order of predominance, go shops of ready-made or made-to-order clothes, fur stores, shops dealing in the most varied foods—an enormous number of confectionaries and bakeries—all belonging to or exploited by staffs of Russian émigrés who have shown themselves at their best in the manufacturing and retailing of shoes. Also in the same business are the small vodka stores, mineral waters, brew kvas, milk products, have stores of pharmacies, etc. Besides these, there are tailors, cobblers, watchmakers, photographers, hairdressers, etc. In addition to all this there are those walking workshops and stores which are usually carried on the shoulders of their salesman and proprietor: the knife-grinders, an echo of the once-existent army of knife-grinders in Russia, who sharpen all sorts of knives, scissors, razors and anything else you give them; men trading in blankets or perfumery; men calling on houses with books or magazines, or trying to sell pictures or even Russian cigarettes, cheese and sausages imported from Harbin.

they tan skins, with the help of the Chinese they have organized their own small mints which turn out articles of gold and silver; Russians draw icons, make wax-candles, wafers and all the other necessary paraphernalia of the Orthodox church; they hew their own grave-stones and monuments, have their own funeral bureaux, are famed in the field of floriculture, maintain hospitals for animals, have scores if barber-shops—in short there is no branch of any artisan or factory labour in which Russians have not made use of their knowledge, experience and energy.

The most remarkable phase of this is that very often Russians have to compete by, so to speak, hand-made methods with the richest foreign enterprises equipped with the most modern methods, and having excellent distributing organizations. But still Russians do not give up. They struggle on, and if they do not actually conquer competition, they do live on their business.

Many Printers

Many foreigners and many foreign offices now give their books to be bound by Russians in spite of the fact that Chinese labour costs considerably less. International Shanghai can hardly know that there are up to twenty Russian printing plants in the city, which turn out newspapers, magazines, books and even textbooks for local Russian schools. In addition to all this there are those walking workshops and stores which are usually carried on the shoulders of their salesman and proprietor: the knife-grinders, an echo of the once-existent army of knife-grinders in Russia, who sharpen all sorts of knives, scissors, razors and anything else you give them; men trading in blankets or perfumery; men calling on houses with books or magazines, or trying to sell pictures or even Russian cigarettes, cheese and sausages imported from Harbin.

Hospital Work

Dr. D. I. Kazakov, President of the Russian Orthodox Confraternity, has shown statistically in what great measure the work of the Russian Hospital has increased this year. In 1934, the hospital had 856 patients; in 1935 there were 907; in 1936 the number had risen to 939, while in the first half of the year 1937 it had already passed 700. This year the activities of the surgical department were considerably widened. In 1935 there were 109 operations, in 1936 there were 167, while during the first six months of the current year there were already 240 operations. The work of the ambulatory has been likewise greatly increased, as during the first half of this year 3,631 people were treated. The number of patients in the tuberculosis department has grown, and as from the beginning of 1937 the Russian Hospital started to take in drug-addicts. These are principally composed of youngsters who in the vicinity of bars become addicted to drugs while in Harbin. The most modern methods are used, and success has been achieved in curing them.

S!
R
D.S. Lohmatschewsky
(印：S)
gth. J

《字林西报》，1937年8月9日，星期一
23566
5002
// 8 37

在
俄国
侨民区

作者：STROY

俄国人以如此专注甚至焦虑的神情关注着北方局势的演变，这或许看似奇怪。人群迅速聚集在俄文报社门前，围拢在大胆刊登最新事态发展的手写海报周围，热切地讨论着这种或那种可能性。人们对“是否会爆发战争”这一问题表现出如此浓厚的兴趣，并非因为俄国人天生好战甚于爱和平，而是因为在过去十五年里，上海的俄国人通过自己的企业和事业深深扎下了根，以至于如今的战争不仅威胁到他们自身及其家庭，也威胁到他们的生意，而这些生意大多是经过极其艰苦的努力才取得成功的。此时爆发战争尤其令人遗憾，因为直到今年年初，俄国侨民区才感受到上海经济萧条的消退，开始稍感宽慰。

今年春天，许多商人前往日本、美国和巴黎采购货物；许多人投身于修缮和扩建店面的工作——所有这些都是为了如俄国人所说，“全副武装”地迎接即将到来的秋季贸易。另一些人则单纯希望，凭借今年赚取的额外收入，他们可以在避暑胜地休息并积蓄更多精力，但这一切如今都可能迎来悲剧性的终结。商店的货物库存通常不多，需要频繁补货， slightest delay（稍有延误）就会立即给企业带来诸多不便。信贷也非常有限，夏季所需的资金是以高利率短期借入的。俄国顾客对不利的政治变化嗅觉灵敏，因此即使是最微小的动荡，也足以扰乱甚至破坏移民贸易和小工业那高效但始终极其脆弱的运作机制。

俄国商人

俄国商人主要经营杂货以及男女服装用品。其次，按普遍程度排列，有成衣或定制服装店、皮草店、经营各种食品的商店——大量的糖果店和面包房——这些都属于或由俄国流亡者团队经营，他们在鞋类的制造和零售方面展现了最佳水平。同样从事这一行业的还有小型伏特加酒店、矿泉水店、克瓦斯酿造厂、乳制品店、药店等。除此之外，还有裁缝、鞋匠、钟表匠、摄影师、理发师等。除了所有这些，还有那些通常由推销员和店主肩挑背负的移动作坊和店铺：磨刀人，这是俄国曾经存在的庞大磨刀大军的余响，他们磨快各种刀具、剪刀、剃须刀以及你交给他们的任何物品；贩卖毛毯或香水的人；上门推销书籍或杂志的人，或者试图出售画作，甚至是从哈尔滨进口的俄国香烟、奶酪和香肠的人。

他们鞣制皮革，在中国人的帮助下组织了自己的小型铸币厂，生产金银制品；俄国人绘制圣像，制作蜡烛、圣饼以及东正教所需的所有其他必要法器；他们凿刻自己的墓碑和纪念碑，拥有自己的殡仪馆，在花卉栽培领域享有盛誉，维持着动物医院，拥有数十家理发店——简而言之，在任何手工艺或工厂劳动分支中，俄国人都利用了他们的知识、经验和精力。

这方面最引人注目的特点是，俄国人往往不得不以所谓的手工方式，与拥有最现代方法和优秀分销组织的最富裕的外国企业进行竞争。但俄国人并未放弃。他们继续奋斗，即使未能真正战胜竞争，也能依靠自己的生意维持生计。

许多印刷商

尽管中国劳动力成本低得多，但现在许多外国人和许多外国机构都将书籍交给俄国人装订。国际化的上海几乎不知道，市内有多达二十家俄国印刷厂，它们出版报纸、杂志、书籍，甚至为当地俄国学校印制教科书。除此之外，还有那些通常由推销员和店主肩挑背负的移动作坊和店铺：磨刀人，这是俄国曾经存在的庞大磨刀大军的余响，他们磨快各种刀具、剪刀、剃须刀以及你交给他们的任何物品；贩卖毛毯或香水的人；上门推销书籍或杂志的人，或者试图出售画作，甚至是从哈尔滨进口的俄国香烟、奶酪和香肠的人。

医院工作

俄国东正教兄弟会主席 D. I. Kazakov 博士通过统计数据展示了俄国医院今年的工作量大幅增加的情况。1934年，该医院有856名病人；1935年为907名；1936年人数上升至939名，而在1937年上半年，人数已超过700名。今年，外科部门的活动范围大大扩大。1935年进行了109台手术，1936年为167台，而在今年的前六个月，手术量已达240台。门诊部的工作量也大幅增加，因为在今年上半年诊治了3,631人。结核病部的病人数有所增加，并且自1937年初起，俄国医院开始接收吸毒成瘾者。这些人主要是年轻人，他们在哈尔滨的酒吧附近染上毒瘾。医院采用最现代的方法进行治疗，并取得了治愈的成功。

S!
R
D.S. Lohmatschewsky
(印：S)

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, MONDAY, JULY 12, 1937
2.3000

IN THE
RUSSIAN
COLONY

By SIBOV

For the past week interest in Russian Shanghai's 20,000 has been concentrated on one topic—the order of the Chinese authorities forbidding the issuing of passports and visas to Russian emigrants until the latter have paid their income tax for a period of six months from January 1, 1937. Russian emigrants, with all their eighteen years of wandering on foreign strands, have learned to respect existing laws and regulations, and do not favour protests, preferring to submit to the demands of authorities and police silently and without undue criticism. But situations sometimes arise when to carry out a certain regulation becomes extremely difficult, if not impossible. Thus it is, to some, with the present income tax. It was imposed forcibly on Russian emigrants, and, as if intentionally, at a time when Russian prepare to leave for summer resorts. As we have already pointed out in these columns, a summer resort is to Russian not primarily a place of rest and recreation, but is either a continuation of the struggle for their daily bread or a means of repairing health, undermined by heavy work under arduous conditions in a sub-tropical climate. That 75 per cent. of the children in Russian schools who this spring underwent a medical examination were found to be in immediate need of being sent to a summer resort, speaks for the fact that health is a boon of which not many Russians in Shanghai can boast. And here, in such conditions, arises the necessity not only to find the means of leaving Shanghai, but to make an immediate payment of income tax covering a period of six months, and, in some cases, even paying fines for overdrawn passports; as all reductions in regard to passports and visas which Russians have always enjoyed in China, were simultaneously discontinued.

Some Hardships
Chinese authorities cannot be ignorant of the fact that literally scores of Chinese pawnbrokers work in Shanghai for a purely Russian "clientele." In order to leave Shanghai for the summer months Russian nearly always pawn everything of their possession which can be pawned, and in addition draw loans from credit companies. Of this modest sum, which already is barely sufficient to send his wife and children to Tsingtao, the indigent Russian now must leave a large part at the Income Tax Bureau in Kiukiang Road. The writer is familiar with the case of a Russian reporter, who does not earn more than $100 a month, but who, in addition to his income tax for a period of six months, must pay $27 for an overdrawn passport. Meanwhile the man is seriously ill, and his doctors sent him to Lushan. A Russian family which is considered well-to-do lives, at an average, on the husband's salary of about $400. In these circumstances the income tax, amounting to about $78, must at once be paid. Russians contrive to secure at the most a bank-loan of $400, and with this they send their families to Tsingtao for a period of two months. Thus a quarter of the loan, on which high rates of percentage are exacted, must now go to the Income Tax Bureau. These are some of the facts which explain the present agitation around the question of the suddenly introduced income tax. Russians have always agreed that income tax must be paid, but at the same time believe that certain debatable points should

The introduction of income tax has not done away with the necessity of procuring a visa costing $4 a person on going to a closely neighbouring port like, say, Tsingtao. More than that, on arriving a Russian emigrant who has lived in China for the last fifteen or eighteen years, and who thus considers himself a permanent resident of this country must for some unknown reason, once more pay $4.50 per person for a Tsingtao passport! In paying their income tax, Russian emigrants are, neither in the French Concession nor in the Settlement, exempted from their house-taxes and other Municipal taxes which continue as a matter of course. Thus Russian emigrants, the poorest and least secure part of the foreign population of Shanghai, must henceforward pay considerably more taxes than more affluent foreigners.

Russian emigrants, we repeat, are quite willing to pay their income tax, but ask that this income tax be exacted from them when it is exacted from all other non-treaty foreign residents of Shanghai. Why start with the emigrants?

Hot Weather Habits
How and with what do Russians combat the heat? First and foremost, they make use of the habit inherited from their forefathers of drinking hot tea, with either a slice of lemon, or some jam. Russians can drink tea endlessly, and prefer tumblers to cups. Also popular is the national drink kvass, which is brewed from pieces of black bread and yeast in boiled water, the process taking the short period of two days. Previously money could not buy "real Russian kvass" in Shanghai; now the city boasts of several factories and the curse of competition has long since set in. Russians drink kvass not only in its pure form, but use it to make cold summer soups—okroshka, into the making of which go several kinds of cold meat, fresh cucumbers, and hard-boiled eggs; and botvinia, made from kvass, spinach, pieces of sturgeon and ice—a remarkable dish! In addition Russians in summer despatch an incredible amount of ice-cream. Vodka is imbibed sparingly, and only at an ice-cold temperature.

Russo-Gipsy Music
The famous exponent of Russo-gipsy music, Mr. Jurly Morfessi, is expected in Shanghai in the autumn. Although the name of Morfessi was on every one's lips as far back as the days of St. Petersburg before the revolution, time has left no mark on his rich voice nor dimmed the expression and rare sincerity of his singing. Cultured Russians and the famous authors and poets like Pushkin and Tolstoi not only always valued gipsy songs but supported, and in part themselves created, a special genre of Russo-gypsy music. The best exponent of this branch of art is Mr. Morfessi, who to-day is as popular as ever, and whose innumerable records his admirers never tire of hearing.

2.3000

在
俄国
侨民区

作者：西博夫（SIBOV）

过去一周，上海两万名俄侨的关注点集中在一个话题上——中国当局颁布命令，禁止向俄国移民签发护照和签证，直至后者缴清自1937年1月1日起为期六个月的所得税。俄国移民在异国他乡漂泊了十八年，已学会尊重现行的法律法规，不倾向于提出抗议，而是选择默默顺从当局和警方的要求，不过多批评。但有时会出现这种情况：执行某项规定变得极其困难，甚至不可能。目前的所得税对某些人而言便是如此。这项税收是强制向俄国移民征收的，而且似乎是故意选在俄国人准备前往避暑胜地的时候。正如本报此前所指出的，对俄国人来说，避暑胜地主要不是休息和娱乐的地方，要么是为维持生计而继续奋斗的场所，要么是在亚热带气候下因艰苦条件下的繁重工作而受损的健康得以恢复的手段。今年春天接受体检的俄国学校儿童中，有75%被发现急需送往避暑胜地，这一事实说明，健康是上海许多俄国人所无法奢求的福分。而在这样的情况下，不仅要想办法筹集离开上海的费用，还要立即缴纳为期六个月的所得税，在某些情况下，甚至要支付护照超期使用的罚款；因为俄国人以往在中国一直享有的关于护照和签证的所有减免待遇，同时也都被取消了。

一些困境

中国当局不可能不知道这样一个事实：在上海， literally 有数十家中国当铺专门为纯粹的俄国“客户群”服务。为了在夏季月份离开上海，俄国人几乎总是典当所有可以典当的物品，此外还向信贷公司借款。这笔微薄的款项原本仅够送妻儿去青岛，如今这位贫困的俄国人却必须将其中大部分留在九江路的所得税局。笔者熟悉一位俄国记者的案例，他月收入不超过100美元，但除了缴纳六个月的所得税外，还必须为护照超期使用支付27美元。与此同时，此人重病在身，医生建议他去庐山休养。一个被认为生活宽裕的俄国家庭，平均依靠丈夫约400美元的薪水生活。在这种情况下，必须立即缴纳约78美元的所得税。俄国人设法最多只能获得400美元的银行贷款，并用这笔钱送家人去青岛度过两个月。因此，这笔贷款的四分之一——且需支付高额利息——现在必须交给所得税局。这些事实解释了围绕突然开征所得税这一问题所产生的当前动荡。俄国人一直同意必须缴纳所得税，但同时也认为某些争议点应当

开征所得税并未免除在前往如青岛这般邻近港口时每人需花费4美元办理签证的必要。不仅如此，一位在中国居住了十五或十八年、因而自视为该国永久居民的俄国移民，在抵达时，出于某种未知原因，还必须再次为青岛护照每人支付4.50美元！在缴纳所得税的同时，俄国移民无论在法租界还是公共租界，均不免除其房产税和其他市政税，这些税费照常征收。因此，作为上海外籍人口中最贫困且最缺乏保障的部分，俄国移民今后缴纳的税款将远多于较富裕的外国人。

我们重申，俄国移民完全愿意缴纳所得税，但要求在对上海其他所有非条约国外籍居民征收所得税时，再向他们征收。为何单从移民开始？

酷暑习惯

俄国人如何以及用什么来对抗炎热？首先也是最重要的，他们利用从祖先那里继承来的喝热茶的习惯，茶中要么加一片柠檬，要么加一些果酱。俄国人可以无休止地喝茶，并且更喜欢用玻璃杯而不是茶杯。同样流行的是民族饮料格瓦斯（kvass），它是用黑面包块和酵母在沸水中酿造而成的，整个过程只需短短两天。以前在上海有钱也买不到“真正的俄国格瓦斯”；现在这座城市已有几家工厂，竞争的弊端早已显现。俄国人不仅直接饮用格瓦斯，还用它制作冷夏汤——奥克罗什卡（okroshka），制作原料包括几种冷肉、新鲜黄瓜和煮鸡蛋；以及波特维尼亚汤（botvinia），由格瓦斯、菠菜、鲟鱼块和冰制成——这是一道非凡的菜肴！此外，俄国人在夏季还会消耗数量惊人的冰淇淋。伏特加酒喝得很少，且只在冰镇状态下饮用。

俄吉普赛音乐

著名的俄吉普赛音乐诠释者尤尔利·莫尔费西（Jurly Morfessi）先生预计将于秋季抵达上海。尽管早在革命前的圣彼得堡时期，莫尔费西的名字就已家喻户晓，但时光并未在他的浑厚嗓音上留下痕迹，也未削弱他歌声中的表现力和罕见的真诚。有教养的俄国人以及普希金和托尔斯泰等著名作家和诗人，不仅一直珍视吉普赛歌曲，还支持并部分创造了一种特殊的俄吉普赛音乐流派。这一艺术分支的最佳诠释者是莫尔费西先生，他如今依然广受欢迎，他的崇拜者们对他无数的唱片百听不厌。

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, MONDAY, JULY 5, 1937 22843

IN THE
RUSSIAN
COLONY

By Smoy

According to information received in Shanghai, the well-known Russian scientist, Prof. Sergei G. Eliseeff, who is an authority on Buddhism and Japanese literature, has just returned to Peiping from Szechuen. When Prof. Eliseeff was in Shanghai a few months ago, Sapajou drew a cartoon of him for the "N.-C.D.N." On being asked whether he was pleased with the portrait, Prof. Eliseeff said, "The portrait is very talented, but in it I don't resemble an emigrant. An emigrant must always have the corner of his lips drooped down, while Sapajou turned them slightly up, thus giving my features the look not of an emigrant but of a person satisfied with life. A good emigrant," the professor smiled, "has no right to be satisfied with life."

In mentioning this remark, it must be pointed out that although, in the opinion of the esteemed professor, all emigrants should have the corners of their lips drooping down, jokes and anecdotes have always existed in Russian emigration circles, often embellishing truly desperate and straitened circumstances. Emigrants have the knack of laughing good-naturedly at the humourous sides of emigration. The famous author-humorist Teffi recently wrote a witty sketch entitled "At an Emigrant Ball," in which a gentleman attends one in the hope of enjoying himself, but is assailed at every step by scrawny damsels who hold plates in front of him and instantly request that he donate something to the victims of tuberculosis. Other maidens wail plaintively: "Subscribe towards the funeral of an aged author!" Someone else looks pleadingly up and begs him to help the unemployed suicides. In time the man who came to cast off mundane cares falls into a state of acute melancholy, while around him the distracted organizers dash to and fro, frantically but hopelessly trying to create an atmosphere of merriment. Anecdotes about emigrants circulating in emigration circles are innumerable. Here is one: Sipping coffee in a boulevard cafe of gay Paris sat two emigrants. One of them lifted a finger and pointed to a waiter bustling from table to table. "See that man?" he asked. "He used to be an aide-de-camp of the Emperor. And that thin, grey-haired fellow there, mixing cocktails behind the bar? Before the revolution he was the Governor-General of Western Siberia." The other nodded and gazed ruefully at a little poodle tied to the leg of his chair. "Yes," he sighed, "all of us have suffered a fall. Before the revolution my Fifi used to be a Great Dane."

Canards

The Russian colony was unpleasantly surprised by the recurrence of the unverified and totally unfounded reports appearing in certain Chinese newspapers regarding the "activity" of the White Russians in China. Recently one of the more influential of the local Chinese newspapers printed a report from Tientsin to the effect that "divisions" of White Russians appear at certain railway stations of North China and carry on espionage work in the interests of a certain neighbouring power. During the previous week local Chinese evening publications broke all records of mendacity by printing a report that at the house at the corner of Yangtzepoo and Thorburn Roads there lives a Russian who allegedly feeds his four savage dogs on Chinese children—dead and alive. As was illustrated last March, at which time it was stated that Russian spies arrive in China from Manchuria in order to open barber-shops and restaurants and carry on espionage work, certain Chinese circles, in Nanking as well as in Shanghai, tend to give these nonsensical rumours a large measure of credence.

"Fortuna"

Among Russian charitable organizations there exists one which is singularly original—"Fortuna." This society, whose founder and Chairman, Mr. V. K. Vitowsky, was long a teacher and social worker, is in its fourth year of existence and has as its motto the simple aphorism that if every Russian in Shanghai were to donate to this society a monthly sum of 30 coppers, the Russian colony would have no indigents. Unfortunately, however, it has not received so far the support of the public and has to exist on the means which it contrives to collect. What are its problems? It has to sustain any Russian who by chance should fall into a helpless position; it has to feed him, shelter him, find him work. If "Fortuna" should in a day feed, say, 100 men, it would in a year thus have extended help to 36,000 people—all on the 30 coppers donated monthly by every Russian in the city. During the four years of its existence, the society has organized work-shops for mending shoes and linen, bureaux for the translating and transcribing of papers, and has given free medical and dental assistance to the poor. "Fortuna" accepts donations of all sorts—not only in coppers but in old boots, broken furniture, old clothes, cast-away cutlery and books. All this is sorted out, mended, renovated and then either utilized or sold. The chairman of this charitable organization, Mr. Vitowsky, who, although an octogenarian, is full of strength and energy, will be glad to answer any questions on the activities of "Fortuna" put to him by telephoning 72898.

Income Tax

On July 1 the Income Tax Bureau and the Police Department of Greater Shanghai published a joint order in all Russian newspapers, to the effect that not one Russian will be given his passport or visa for travel abroad if he does not pay his income tax and fill in the income tax questionnaire. The tax must, it was stated, be paid as from 1 January 1937, i.e. for a period of six months, which is a stipulation difficult of compliance for the far from well-to-do Russian emigrants.

Some Russians recently attempted to renew their passports at the Bureau of Public Safety at Nantao, but found that this was refused them until such time as they pay their income tax. Previously, the Chinese authorities issued passports to indigent Russians at a generous reduction, and to others of extreme poverty even gave passports free of charge. Now they have stopped doing either.

（批：ts/Profier）
（批：S.1 / 印 / JP lofol7）

《字林西报》，1937年7月5日，星期一 22843

在
俄国
侨民区

作者：Smoy

据上海收到的消息，著名的俄国科学家、佛教及日本文学权威谢尔盖·G·叶利谢耶夫（Sergei G. Eliseeff）教授刚从四川返回北平。几个月前叶利谢耶夫教授在上海时，萨帕茹（Sapajou）曾为《字林西报》绘制了一幅他的漫画。当被问及是否满意这幅肖像时，叶利谢耶夫教授说：“这幅画很有才气，但在画中我不像个流亡者。流亡者的嘴角必须总是下垂的，而萨帕茹却将我的嘴角微微上扬，从而使我的面容看起来不像个流亡者，倒像个对生活感到满足的人。一个合格的流亡者，”教授微笑着说，“没有权利对生活感到满足。”

在提及这番言论时，必须指出的是，尽管在这位受人尊敬的教授看来，所有流亡者的嘴角都应当下垂，但在俄国流亡圈子里，笑话和轶事一直存在，往往为真正绝望和困窘的境遇增添色彩。流亡者擅长以善意的心态嘲笑流亡生活中幽默的一面。著名幽默作家泰菲（Teffi）最近写了一篇题为《在流亡者舞会上》的机智小品，文中一位绅士参加舞会希望能享受乐趣，但每一步都受到瘦弱少女的纠缠，她们端着盘子挡在他面前，立刻请求他为肺结核受害者捐款。其他少女则哀怨地哭诉：“请为一位年迈作家的葬礼捐款！”还有人乞求地看着他，恳请他帮助那些失业的自杀者。久而久之，这位本想摆脱世俗烦恼的人陷入了极度的忧郁之中，而周围那些焦头烂额的组织者则跑来跑去，疯狂却徒劳地试图营造欢乐的气氛。在流亡圈子里流传的关于流亡者的轶事数不胜数。这里有一则：在繁华巴黎的林荫大道咖啡馆里，两名流亡者正在啜饮咖啡。其中一人抬起手指，指向一名在桌间忙碌穿梭的服务员。“看见那个人了吗？”他问道。“他曾经是皇帝的副官。还有那边那个在吧台后调制鸡尾酒的瘦削灰发男子？革命前他是西西伯利亚总督。”另一人点点头，悲哀地凝视着绑在他椅腿上的一只小贵宾犬。“是啊，”他叹息道，“我们大家都遭遇了落魄。革命前，我的菲菲（Fifi）曾是一只大丹犬。”

谣言

某些中文报纸上再次出现未经证实且毫无根据的报道，称在华“白俄”有某种“活动”，这令俄国侨民区感到不悦。最近，当地一家较有影响力的中文报纸刊登了一则来自天津的报道，声称“白俄”的“师团”出现在华北某些火车站，并为某个邻国利益从事间谍活动。上周，当地中文晚报打破了撒谎的记录，刊登报道称，在杨树浦路与索伯恩路（Thorburn Roads）拐角处的一所房子里，住着一名俄国人，据说他用中国儿童——无论是死的还是活的——喂养他的四条猛犬。正如去年三月所显示的那样，当时声称俄国间谍从满洲抵达中国，开设理发店和餐馆以从事间谍工作，南京和上海的一些中国圈子倾向于对这些荒谬的谣言给予很大程度的信任。

“福图纳”（Fortuna）

在俄国慈善组织中，有一个组织格外独特——“福图纳”。该协会由长期担任教师和社会工作者的V. K·维托夫斯基（V. K. Vitowsky）先生创立并担任主席，目前已成立四年，其座右铭是一句简单的格言：如果上海的每位俄国人每月向该协会捐赠30枚铜板，那么俄国侨民区将不再有贫民。然而不幸的是，该协会迄今未获得公众的支持，只能依靠其设法筹集的资金维持运作。它面临哪些问题？它必须资助任何偶然陷入无助境地的俄国人；必须供养他、为他提供住所、为他寻找工作。如果“福图纳”一天能供养例如100人，那么一年下来它将以此方式帮助36,000人——这一切都基于该市每位俄国人每月捐赠的30枚铜板。在成立的四年间，该协会组织了修补鞋类和亚麻织品的工场，设立了文件翻译和抄写办事处，并向穷人提供免费医疗和牙科援助。“福图纳”接受各种捐赠——不仅是铜板，还包括旧靴子、破损家具、旧衣服、废弃餐具和书籍。所有这些东西经过分类、修补、翻新，然后要么加以利用，要么出售。该慈善组织的主席维托夫斯基先生虽已年过八旬，但精力充沛，如有任何人通过电话72898向他询问有关“福图纳”活动的问题，他将乐意作答。

所得税

7月1日，大上海所得税局与警察局在所有俄文报纸上联合发布命令，称任何俄国人若不缴纳所得税并填写所得税问卷，将不予签发护照或出国签证。命令指出，税款必须从1937年1月1日起缴纳，即为期六个月，这一规定对于远非富裕的俄国流亡者来说难以遵守。

最近，一些俄国人试图在南市公共安全局更新护照，但发现除非缴纳所得税，否则申请将被拒绝。此前，中国当局以大幅优惠的价格向贫困俄国人签发护照，甚至对极度贫困者免费发放护照。现在他们已停止这两种做法。

（批：ts/Profier）
（批：S.1 / 印 / JP lofol7）

IN THE
RUSSIAN
COLONY

By SMOY

Russian names, or names resembling Russian, appear quite often in the pages of Shanghai chronicles of crime. Does that mean that the percentage of criminals among Russians is higher than that among other nationalities? People near to the business of the courts repudiate this. Capt. Barrett, former Commissioner of Police, stated on retirement that the percentage of criminals among Russians is exceptionally trivial. He was, of course, speaking of the 20,000 law-abiding Russian citizens who have established themselves permanently in Shanghai and who depend on honest work to feed themselves and their families. After the altered conditions in Manchukuo, however, when the depression hit the main centres of the Far East—centres like Mukden, Tientsin and Hankow—criminals of all sorts and standings flocked to Shanghai. Among them were Russians—but these could be more truly called representatives of the international world of crime.

When Russians figure on the criminal side of court proceedings, they generally appear because of fights and quarrels—quarrels often begun while in a drunken state and developed from mere trifles. Due to the ease with which cases can be brought in Chinese criminal courts, the injured party often does so: solely from considerations of principle—to satisfy his wounded self-esteem. Into the second category fall cases of fraudulence and misappropriation—typical of local conditions on which minor trade, subsisting largely on small amounts of credit, is built. Russians often launch into business without capital, which they cannot acquire anywhere, go into debt for premises and goods, are at every step unable to pay Customs for imported merchandise and, hoping to disentangle themselves, sell their goods for a mere song, at the same time incurring obligations which they are unable to fulfil and issuing cheques for which they have insufficient funds.

With the ease with which Shanghai law transforms a civil case into a criminal one, and with the unwillingness of the victimised party to give the debtor time to improve his business, minor court cases are frequent. Shanghai creditors are, as a rule, exceptionally quick to react to any delay in payments, court procedure is very rapid, Russian lawyers are plentiful, and so the casual observer involuntarily receives the impression that the Russian colony is filled with crooks of every description.

In considering other reasons why Russians appear in court, there are robberies, mostly minor ones, which are born of want. In short, the crimes which would be committed by professional criminals are very rare in the Russian colony.

There is yet another form of offence, typical of Shanghai: the offence of deserting the family. There are some men who think that when they arrive at such a big and heterogeneous city as Shanghai, it is not a very hard matter to leave their wives, and even children, to their own destiny. Chinese authorities usually display much gentleness in cases of this sort. Local laws deal very sternly with such people. But there have even been cases when alimony was exacted for ordinary cohabitation. It sometimes occurs that a person puts some woman into his passport as his wife—if only for convenience in travel. On arriving at Shanghai this fictitious husband naturally prepares to plan his life as he sees fit—and here it is that his pseudo wife makes him answer for his indiscretion. But such cases are rare.

Church Holiday

Last week Russian churches celebrated the holiday of the Holy Trinity and the Holy Spirit. This falls on the 8th week—or 50th day—after the resurrection of Our Lord. On this day the Orthodox Church recalls all the deceased Orthodox Christians, and prays specially for those who died suddenly, without absolution. The chief feature of this holiday is that in the morning, after mass, vespers are at once held; and the priest, on his knees at the door of the sanctuary, three times utters the prayers of St. Basil the Great. On this day it is the Russian custom to decorate churches and houses with flowers: there are flowers on walls, flowers on ikons, the worshippers stand with flowers in their hands, and fresh green grass softly blankets the floor.

Musician's Tribute

An interesting thought was given by the well-known violinist, Michael Piastro, who last Thursday gave a concert with A. Mirovitch, pianist, and Schuster, cellist. Questioned as to whether he had given concerts in the U.S.S.R., Mr. Piastro said: "Actually, one need not go to the U.S.S.R. to be among Russians. We gave concerts before Russians all over the world; and here in Shanghai a large number of Russians were also present at our concert. The Russian audience is very attentive, impressionable and most enthusiastic about serious music. I can only say this: if Russian audiences were suddenly to disappear from the concert halls of the world, their absence would be sorely felt by us artists."

Boxer Popular

Prior to the war of 1914, Russians, and especially the older generation, were very indifferent to sport. At any rate, sport in Russia never played the role it does in England and America. Now times are changing. The arrival of the young Russian boxer, Andrei Sheleff illustrated that the former lukewarmness has disappeared. Apart from the fact whether this Russian lad should fulfill their hopes or not, on the days when he is to fight, Russian Shanghai talks only of him. In the streets, in shops, in Russian clubs, at parties, everywhere and always, among the old and the young, it is the same—Sheleff. Newspapers devote whole pages to him; every detail of his short 17-year-old life is common knowledge; and his photographs are everywhere. Interest in other forms of sport is also growing, but tennis still seems to have the upper hand. The younger generation is taking up skating, and only golf, even in Shanghai, has hardly any adherents. This is explained by the fact that Russians claim golf is too costly a recreation. The most popular forms of sport in Russia are skating and skiing, and, of course, out of the question in Shanghai.

D.S.S Prokofieff

在
俄国
侨民区

作者：SMOY

俄国人的名字，或看似俄国人的名字，经常出现在上海犯罪纪事的版面上。这是否意味着俄国人中的罪犯比例高于其他国籍？熟悉法庭事务的人士对此予以否认。前警务处处长巴雷特（Barrett）上尉在退休时曾表示，俄国人中的罪犯比例微乎其微。他当然指的是那两万名已在上海永久定居、依靠诚实劳动养活自己和家人的守法俄国公民。然而，在满洲国局势变化之后，当经济萧条冲击远东的主要中心——如沈阳、天津和汉口等地时，各种类型和层级的罪犯纷纷涌入上海。其中也有俄国人——但这些人更确切地说应被称为国际犯罪界的代表。

当俄国人出现在法庭诉讼的被告席上时，通常是因为斗殴和争吵——这些争吵往往始于醉酒状态，并由琐事升级而成。由于在中国刑事法庭提起诉讼十分容易，受害方常常这样做：纯粹是出于原则考虑——以抚慰其受伤的自尊心。第二类案件是欺诈和挪用公款，这是当地环境的典型特征，当地的小本贸易主要建立在小额信贷的基础上。俄国人经常在没有任何资本的情况下投身商界，而他们在任何地方都无法获得资本；他们为租赁场所和购买商品而举债，在每一步都无力支付进口货物的关税，并希望通过低价抛售货物来摆脱困境，同时却背负了无法履行的债务，并开出空头支票。

鉴于上海法律能轻易将民事案件转化为刑事案件，加之受害方不愿给债务人改善经营的时间，小型法庭案件屡见不鲜。上海的债权人通常对任何付款延误反应极快，法庭程序非常迅速，俄国律师又为数众多，因此旁观者不禁会产生一种印象，认为俄国侨民区充斥着各类骗子。

在考虑俄国人出庭的其他原因时，还有抢劫案，大多为轻微抢劫，皆因贫困所致。简言之，职业罪犯所犯下的罪行在俄国侨民区极为罕见。

还有一种上海特有的违法行为：遗弃家庭。有些人认为，当他们来到像上海这样庞大且多元的城市时，抛弃妻子甚至子女，任其自生自灭，并非难事。中国当局在此类案件中通常表现得相当温和。地方法律对此类人处理严厉。但甚至有过判决要求为普通同居关系支付赡养费的案例。有时会出现这种情况：某人为了旅行方便，将一名女子作为妻子登记在护照上。抵达上海后，这位名义上的丈夫自然准备按自己的意愿规划生活——而此时，他的伪妻子便让他为自己的轻率行为付出代价。但此类案例实属罕见。

教会节日

上周，俄国教堂庆祝了圣三一节和圣灵降临节。这一节日落在主复活后的第八周——即第五十天。在这一天，东正教会纪念所有已故的东正教基督徒，并特别为那些未及忏悔而突然去世的人祈祷。这个节日的主要特点是，早晨弥撒结束后，立即举行晚祷；神父跪在圣所门口，三次诵念圣大巴西略（St. Basil the Great）的祷文。在这一天，俄国有用鲜花装饰教堂和房屋的习俗：墙上饰有鲜花，圣像上饰有鲜花，信徒们手持鲜花站立，新鲜的绿草轻柔地铺满地面。

音乐家的致敬

著名小提琴家米哈伊尔·皮亚斯特罗（Michael Piastro）提出了一個有趣的观点。上周四，他与钢琴家A.米罗维奇（A. Mirovitch）和大提琴手舒斯特（Schuster）共同举办了一场音乐会。当被问及是否在苏联举办过音乐会时，皮亚斯特罗先生说：“实际上，不必去苏联也能身处俄国人之中。我们在世界各地的俄国人面前举办过音乐会；在上海，也有大量俄国人出席了我们的音乐会。俄国观众非常专注、敏感，并对严肃音乐表现出极大的热情。我只能说这一点：如果俄国观众突然从世界各音乐厅消失，我们艺术家将会深切感受到他们的缺席。”

拳击手受欢迎

在1914年战争之前，俄国人，尤其是老一代人，对体育运动非常冷漠。无论如何，体育在俄国从未像在英美那样扮演重要角色。现在时代正在改变。年轻俄国拳击手安德烈·谢列夫（Andrei Sheleff）的到来表明，以往的冷淡态度已经消失。不管这位俄国青年能否实现人们的期望，在他比赛的那些日子里，上海俄国人谈论的只有他。在街道上、商店里、俄国俱乐部中、聚会上，无论老少，处处人人都在谈论——谢列夫。报纸整版报道他；他短短17年人生中的每个细节都为人所知；他的照片随处可见。人们对其他体育形式的兴趣也在增长，但网球似乎仍占上风。年轻一代开始从事滑冰运动，而即使在上海，高尔夫球也几乎没有什么追随者。这是因为俄国人认为高尔夫是一项过于昂贵的娱乐活动。俄国最流行的体育项目是滑冰和滑雪，当然，这些在上海是无法进行的。

D.S.S 普罗科菲耶夫（Prokofieff）

IN THE RUSSIAN COLONY

By Smoy

What is the divorce situation in Russian Shanghai? Generally speaking, the same as anywhere else. It cannot be said that divorces among Russians are frequent, but the very character of the divorce cases is typical of Shanghai and Shanghai only. In local courts the most frequent grounds for divorce are the unknown whereabouts of one of the parties—generally the husband. The revolution in Russia, and resultant exile of twenty years, have together wrecked many a Russian family. The husband remained in the homeland or set out to try his luck in America or Australia; the years have passed, and the wife who stayed in Shanghai has now built up her own life and wants to be free in the eyes of the law. Then there are divorces brought with the mutual consent of the husband and wife. The official grounds are given as incompatibility. Here the motive is a purely economic one. When such cases are heard some extremely interesting details are often brought to light. Many marry young, having no clear perception how the life of newly-married must be planned to meet the conditions brought about by the fight for daily bread in emigration. Here it is that "incompatibility" is rapidly discovered, all the more acute when the husband has not the means for a sufficiently comfortable life. Shanghai in its European section, with its high standard of living, produces higher demands; and when the Russian husband with his modest salary is unable to satisfy these demands, the thought of divorce at once presents itself. After that the wife lives her own life as she wishes. Often she pays cruelly for being tempted by the city lights. Sometimes the reason for the divorce is a proposed marriage with a foreigner. In such cases a court divorce is compulsory, as the Consular Courts, where the marriages of Russians with foreigners are registered, demand formal documents. It sometimes happens that marriages with foreigners lead to further divorces; and this time the divorce must take place in a Consular Court, which entails much greater expense than in a Chinese one. In divorces from foreign husbands alimony is always awarded, but only if the husband can be located. If he has a job, and if his place of residence is known. Unfortunately, however, it often so happens in Shanghai that the husband, cutting himself off from the family, at the same time cuts the family off from their means of subsistence by leaving for an unknown destination. Nowadays, however, it is becoming more and more frequent for Russians to marry Russians, and the desire to wed a foreigner at all costs is rapidly passing. The cases of women already married to Russian people, in Shanghai, who have asked for divorce on grounds of cruelty or gross treatment are exceedingly rare. In general, the Russian community suffers principally from social-economic reasons.

Russians in California

A profusely illustrated and interesting album under the title "Fort Ross" has just been published in Shanghai. It tells the story of the colonising of California a hundred years ago by Russians. In the year 1811 or 1812, 120 Russian soldiers and 200 aborigines of Alaska, under the leadership of Lieut. Ivan Kuskov, took possession of the Bay of Bodega and the basin of the river which is still known as Russian River, and built a fort whose remains, carefully preserved by Americans can be seen to this day. By an edict of Emperor Alexander I, the shores of the Pacific Ocean, including many islands from 45 degrees North Latitude and land on the American continent from 51 degrees, were declared Russian territory and the entry of foreign ships into this zone was forbidden. This caused a lengthy conflict with the United States of America. In December, 1841, Fort Ross was sold to one John A. Sutter for $30,000, to be paid over a period of four years. To-day Fort Ross is one of the National Parks of America and is under care and supervision of the Historic Landmarks Committee, Native Sons of the Golden West, whose work is greatly appreciated by Russians.

Prince's Death

The sad information has been received at Shanghai, that the Duke of Leichtenberg, Prince Beauharnais, the brother of the Duchess of Leichtenberg who recently gave a concert at Shanghai in the American Women's Club, died in Munchen. The Duke passed away suddenly, being only 40 years of age, and is survived by his wife and two children. He was a Cavalry Officer of the Imperial Guards, and was in the ranks of the Russian Army during the war. After the revolution he resided in France and Germany, where he graduated from a Conservatory, being possessed of considerable musical talent. He was a composer, and could play the piano, violin, 'cello and other instruments, and even formed a choir composed of ex-officers, which gave concerts in many of the principal cities of Europe and enjoyed great popularity. On Saturday an obituary service was held in the Russian Cathedral, at which the sister and the cousin of the Duke of Leichtenberg, the Baroness of Meiller-Zakomelsky, many of the Russian nobility, and officers of the "Guards" and other illustrious regiments were present.

Artists Return

Several days ago Mme. O Orlova-Kaya, prima donna of the Russian Light Opera, and Miss Helen Orlova, the well-known ballerina, returned from Colombo. Besides that city they, together with other Russian artists from Shanghai under the direction of the balletmaster, D. Fokin, gave recitals in Bombay and Calcutta. The Russian artists, most of whom saw India and the island of Ceylon for the first time, were full of enthusiasm over their tour, told with rapture their impressions, and brought back many interesting photographs. Familiar to the patrons of the Russian Light Opera, Mr. Vain, comedian, and Mr. Fokin, did some big game hunting in the jungle. Unfortunately one of their number, Mr. Luntsed, a young tenor, fell ill with typhoid fever in Bombay. During the Coronation festivities the Russian artists were invited to perform for the public everywhere—and especially for the public in particular. The programme of the tour has been retained by all.

在俄侨聚居区

作者：Smoy

上海俄侨的离婚状况如何？总体而言，与其他地方并无二致。不能说俄国人离婚频繁，但离婚案件本身的性质却是上海所独有的典型特征。在地方法院中，最常见的离婚理由是一方（通常是丈夫）下落不明。俄国的革命以及随之而来的二十年流亡生活，共同摧毁了许多俄国人的家庭。丈夫留在祖国，或者前往美国或澳大利亚碰运气；岁月流逝，留在上海的妻子已经建立了自己的生活，希望在法律上获得自由身份。此外，还有夫妻双方同意离婚的情况。官方给出的理由是性格不合。这里的动机纯粹是经济性的。在审理此类案件时，往往会披露一些极其有趣的细节。许多人年轻结婚，对于新婚生活应如何规划以适应移民后为生计奔波的状况，缺乏清晰的认识。在这种情况下，“性格不合”很快便显现出来，而当丈夫没有能力维持足够舒适的生活时，这种矛盾尤为尖锐。上海欧洲人居住区的生活水平较高，由此产生了更高的需求；当收入微薄的俄国丈夫无法满足这些需求时，离婚的念头便立刻浮现。此后，妻子便按自己的意愿过活。她常常因受城市灯红酒绿的诱惑而付出惨痛的代价。有时，离婚的原因是为了与外国人再婚。在此类情况下，法院判决离婚是强制性的，因为负责登记俄国人与外国人婚姻的领事法庭要求提供正式文件。有时，与外国人的婚姻会导致进一步的离婚；而这一次，离婚必须在领事法庭进行，其费用远高于在中国法庭离婚。在与外国丈夫离婚的案件中，总会判给赡养费，但前提是能找到丈夫。即他要有工作，且居住地已知。然而不幸的是，在上海经常发生这样的情况：丈夫切断与家庭的联系，同时因前往未知目的地而使家庭失去生计来源。不过，如今俄国人之间通婚的情况越来越普遍，不惜一切代价嫁给外国人的愿望正在迅速消退。在上海，已嫁给俄国人的妇女以遭受残酷对待或恶劣待遇为由申请离婚的案例极为罕见。总体而言，俄侨社区主要遭受社会经济原因的困扰。

加利福尼亚的俄国人

上海刚刚出版了一本插图丰富、趣味盎然的相册，题为《罗斯堡》。它讲述了一百年前俄国人殖民加利福尼亚的故事。1811年或1812年，在伊万·库斯科夫（Ivan Kuskov）中尉的率领下，120名俄国士兵和200名阿拉斯加土著居民占领了博德加湾（Bay of Bodega）及至今仍被称为“俄罗斯河”（Russian River）的河流流域，并建造了一座堡垒，其遗迹经美国人精心保存，至今可见。根据亚历山大一世皇帝的敕令，太平洋沿岸，包括北纬45度起的许多岛屿以及美洲大陆北纬51度起的土地，被宣布为俄国领土，禁止外国船只进入该区域。这导致了与美国长期的冲突。1841年12月，罗斯堡以3万美元的价格出售给约翰·A·萨特（John A. Sutter），分四年付清。如今，罗斯堡是美国国家公园之一，由“金色西部本土之子”协会的历史地标委员会负责管理和监督，其工作深受俄国人赞赏。

亲王逝世

上海收到噩耗，莱希滕伯格公爵（Duke of Leichtenberg）、博阿尔内亲王（Prince Beauharnais）在慕尼黑去世。他是近期在上海美国女子俱乐部举办音乐会的莱希滕伯格女公爵的兄弟。公爵突然离世，年仅40岁，遗孀及两名子女尚在。他曾是帝国卫队的骑兵军官，战争期间在俄国军队服役。革命后，他居住在法国和德国，并在那里从音乐学院毕业，颇具音乐天赋。他是一位作曲家，能演奏钢琴、小提琴、大提琴及其他乐器，甚至组建了一个由前军官组成的合唱团，在欧洲许多主要城市举行音乐会，广受欢迎。周六，在俄国大教堂举行了追悼仪式，莱希滕伯格公爵的姐妹、梅勒-扎科梅尔斯基男爵夫人（Baroness of Meiller-Zakomelsky）、众多俄国贵族以及“卫队”和其他著名军团的军官出席了仪式。

艺术家归来

数日前，俄国轻歌剧团首席女高音奥尔洛娃-卡娅夫人（Mme. O Orlova-Kaya）和著名芭蕾舞女演员海伦·奥尔洛娃小姐（Miss Helen Orlova）从科伦坡返回。除该城市外，她们还与上海的其他俄国艺术家一起，在芭蕾大师D·福金（D. Fokin）的指导下，在孟买和加尔各答举行了独奏会。大多数首次见到印度和锡兰岛的俄国艺术家对此次巡演充满热情，欣喜地讲述了他们的印象，并带回了许多有趣的照片。俄国轻歌剧团的赞助人所熟悉的喜剧演员韦恩先生（Mr. Vain）和福金先生（Mr. Fokin）在丛林中进行了一次大型狩猎。不幸的是，他们中的一员，年轻的男高音伦策德先生（Mr. Luntsed），在孟买患上了伤寒。在加冕庆典期间，俄国艺术家受邀在各种场合——特别是为特定公众——进行演出。此次巡演的节目单被所有人保留了下来。

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, MONDAY, SHANGHAI MUNICIPAL 1937

IN THE
RUSSIAN
COLONY

By STROY

Due to altered conditions in Manchuria, many Russian lawyers have in recent years transferred their practice from Harbin to Shanghai. Before this, they had over ten years' practice in Chinese courts, and thus possess wide experience, together with a first-hand knowledge of Chinese laws and the customs and peculiarities of court procedure. Of special interest are their views on Chinese courts in Shanghai compared with corresponding courts in Manchuria. They are fully satisfied with the rapidity of law-proceedings—the majority of verdicts are here reached after one or two sittings—but they find it new to them that in Shanghai there is an almost complete absence of preliminary investigation, and that the part played by the procurator is an extremely small one. It is very characteristic of Chinese courts in Shanghai that often cases which from the point of view of Russian jurists clearly bear a civil character—as, for instance, private monetary dealings—in Shanghai have sometimes first to pass through a list of criminal offences, being brought into court on charges of breach of confidence or even fraudulence. Also characteristic of Shanghai is the fact that both non-payment of cheques and the giving out of cheques without sufficient money to cover them, are similarly counted as criminal offences.

It is sometimes the case that in Chinese courts there is no experienced interpreter and the lawyer has to employ one of his own; this, of course, makes the handling of a case still more expensive. Court tariffs in Shanghai slightly exceed those in Harbin. But the most interesting peculiarity of Shanghai Law is the number of local Chinese courts: The Shanghai District Court in Nantao subordinated to the High Court at Soochow; the First District Court in the Settlement, and the Second District Court in the French Concession, both of which are subordinated to the 2nd and 3rd Divisions of the High Court at Kiangsu. While all these courts are part of the Government judicial system yet cases in them are judged separately. The work of lawyers in Shanghai is made still more difficult by the absence of addresses. A debtor sometimes manages to live in Shanghai for years, adroitly changing his places of residence and concealing his address; and this wholly escapes the necessity of paying his debts. If a debtor who has lost a case in the French Concession, moves into the Settlement, he has to be located once more and if after that he managed to slip into Chinese territory, it becomes still more difficult to find him there.

Children Unhealthy

The Medical Committee, which is organizing the sending of sick Russian children to summer camps in the interior provinces, reports that Dr. P. I. Orlov and Dr. C. A. Gurevich were recently visiting the children of the Russian colonies in Shanghai. The results of their examination were published last week. Out of 500 children examined, 300 were found to be in need of rest in a summer resort. The committee has so far enough funds to send only 150, while in order to save many young lives no less than 300 will have to be sent. The local representative of the League of Nations has donated $2,200 to the National Committee for this children's camp, the French Consul-General has allotted $2,000. Sir Victor Sassoon has generously aided with $500, a collection has been started among Russians. It is hoped that the shipping companies, Jardine, Matheson & Co. and Butterfield & Swire will help by quoting reduced rates—but even so this money will not be enough to maintain for two months a camp numbering 300. The National Committee has appealed to the Rotary Club and would like to appeal to their foreign friends to help as far as they can in this worthy undertaking, as the enormous amount of sick children in Russian schools, ascertained by the latest medical investigation, is a threat to the health of the whole city.

New Magazine

"Russian Annals," the first and only large Russian magazine—not only in Shanghai but in the whole of the Far East—will make its appearance on June 20. This magazine is the continuation of "Contemporary Annals," the most popular magazine among Russians abroad, which for a period of fifteen years was published in Paris, and which due to the increase in the cost of production recently terminated its existence. The new journal's Board of Editors is composed of the same people who made such a success of the first one, while among the permanent contributors are numbered the most famous of Russian authors and philosophers such as Ivan Bunin, winner of the 1933 Nobel Prize for Literature, D. S. Merejkowski, M. Aldanov, the most popular of emigrant novelists, Boris Zaitzeff, Prof. N. A. Berdyaeff, and others. In addition to these there are among the new contributors persons well known in the Far East: Prof. G. G. Telberg, an expert on the history of the Russian Law and former Minister of Justice, at present settled in Tsingtao, and B. V. Ostroumoff, a brilliant engineer, famous for his achievements while during the years 1921-1925 he was, after General Horvath, General Manager of the Chinese Eastern Railway. The new magazine has as one of its aims the publication of problems in the Far East and around the Pacific Ocean, and will furthermore devote large attention to the centres of Russian emigration in America. The journal will appear six times a year and will have a volume of 280 pages. Into exile from Russia went many well known authors and publicists; and in addition to these, a new, young generation of writers has formed during twenty years. But although in some places—as, for instance, in Shanghai, where printing expenses are so small—it is not so costly to publish a book, it is very difficult and expensive for a small publisher or what is more, for an individual writer, to distribute such a book—to reach Russian readers scattered throughout the world. That is why the possibility of establishing a new magazine, which will be distributed wherever Russians are found, is enticing young Russian authors.

D.S.J Prokofiev
JL

《字林西报》，星期一，上海公共租界，1937年

在
俄国
侨民区

作者：STROY

由于满洲局势的变化，近年来许多俄国律师将其执业地点从哈尔滨转移至上海。在此之前，他们已在中国法院拥有超过十年的执业经验，因此具备丰富的阅历，并对中国法律以及法庭程序的习惯与特点有着第一手的了解。特别引人关注的是，他们将上海的中國法院与满洲的相应法院进行了比较后的观点。他们对诉讼程序的迅速感到完全满意——大多数判决在此经过一两次开庭即可达成——但他们发现，在上海几乎完全没有预审调查，且检察官所起的作用极小，这对他们来说是新鲜事。上海的中国法院的一个显著特征是，从俄国法学家角度来看明显具有民事性质的案件——例如私人金钱往来——在上海有时必须先经过一系列刑事罪名的程序，以违背信任甚至欺诈的指控被诉至法庭。上海的另一个典型事实是，支票拒付以及开具空头支票（即没有足够资金兑付的支票）同样被视为刑事犯罪。

有时会出现中国法院没有经验丰富的译员的情况，律师不得不自行聘请译员；这当然使得案件处理更加昂贵。上海的法院费用略高于哈尔滨。但上海法律最有趣的特殊性在于当地中国法院的数量：位于南市、隶属于苏州高等法院的上海地方法院；位于租界的第一地方法院，以及位于法租界的第二地方法院，后两者均隶属于江苏高等法院的第二和第三分院。虽然所有这些法院都是政府司法体系的一部分，但其中的案件是分别审理的。地址信息的缺失使律师在上海的工作变得更加困难。债务人有时能在上海居住多年，巧妙地更换居住地并隐藏其地址；从而完全逃避了偿还债务的必要。如果一名在法租界败诉的债务人搬入公共租界，就必须重新查找其下落；而如果此后他又设法潜入华界，在那里找到他就变得更加困难。

儿童健康状况不佳

负责组织将患病俄国儿童送往内地省份夏令营的医疗委员会报告称，P. I. Orlov 博士和 C. A. Gurevich 博士最近走访了上海俄国侨民区的儿童。他们的检查结果于上周公布。在接受检查的500名儿童中，有300人被认为需要去避暑胜地休养。委员会目前的资金仅够派遣150人，而为了挽救许多年轻的生命，至少需要派遣300人。国际联盟的本地代表向该儿童夏令营的国家委员会捐赠了2,200美元，法国总领事拨款2,000美元。维克多·沙逊爵士（Sir Victor Sassoon）慷慨资助了500美元，俄国人中也发起了一场募捐活动。希望航运公司怡和洋行（Jardine, Matheson & Co.）和太古洋行（Butterfield & Swire）能通过提供优惠费率来提供帮助——但即便如此，这笔钱也不足以维持一个拥有300人的夏令营达两个月之久。国家委员会已向扶轮社发出呼吁，并希望向其外国朋友呼吁，在这一值得进行的事业中尽其所能提供帮助，因为最新的医学调查证实，俄国学校中患病儿童数量巨大，这对整个城市的健康构成了威胁。

新杂志

《俄国年鉴》（Russian Annals）是第一本也是唯一一本大型俄国杂志——不仅在上海，而且在整个远东地区——将于6月20日问世。这本杂志是《当代年鉴》（Contemporary Annals）的延续，《当代年鉴》是海外俄国人中最受欢迎的杂志，在巴黎出版了十五年，最近由于生产成本增加而停刊。新期刊的编委会由使第一期杂志取得巨大成功的同一批人组成，而其固定撰稿人中包括最著名的俄国作家和哲学家，如1933年诺贝尔文学奖得主伊万·布宁（Ivan Bunin）、D. S. Merejkowski、M. Aldanov（最受欢迎的流亡小说家之一）、Boris Zaitzeff、N. A. Berdyaeff 教授等。除了这些人之外，新撰稿人中还有在远东知名的人士：G. G. Telberg 教授，俄国法律史专家及前司法部长，现定居青岛；以及 B. V. Ostroumoff，一位杰出的工程师，因其在1921-1925年间继霍瓦特将军（General Horvath）之后担任中东铁路总经理期间的成就而闻名。新杂志的目标之一是出版有关远东及太平洋地区问题的文章，此外还将大量关注美洲的俄国移民中心。该期刊每年出版六期，每卷篇幅为280页。许多著名作家和政论家流亡出俄国；除此之外，在过去二十年中又形成了新一代的年轻作家群体。但是，尽管在某些地方——例如上海，那里的印刷费用非常低廉——出版书籍的成本并不高，但对于小型出版商，或者更确切地说，对于个体作家而言，分发此类书籍——以触及散居世界各地的俄国读者——是非常困难且昂贵的。这就是为什么建立一本新杂志的可能性吸引着年轻的俄国作家，该杂志将发行到所有有俄国人的地方。

D.S.J Prokofiev
JL

2172
IN THE
RUSSIAN
COLONY
500
By STROY
Russian Shanghai is eagerly interested in the Coronation festivities. Russians have always remembered that King Edward VII and Emperor Alexander III were married to two sisters. It is not easy to judge what were the causes which resulted in antagonism between the two nations in the 19th century and even led to the Crimean war, but from the beginning of the reign of King Edward VII, the goodwill of the Russian public began to veer decisively toward England. The meeting of the two sovereigns Edward VII and Nicholas II in Revel laid the foundation for a friendship which continued to the very end of the imperial epoch in Russia. Russians only a few weeks ago read with great interest an historical essay which told of the glowing friendship which sprang up about 100 years ago between Queen Victoria and the heir apparent to the Russian throne, Tsarevitch Alexander Nicholaevitch, later Czar Alexander II, who at that time was visiting London on a mission for his father, Emperor Nicholas I.
Though at first under the influence of French culture and then under that of Germany, Russians have nevertheless always valued not only English culture but English civilization as well. English merchandise—cloth, steel, etc.,—were always counted as best by Russians; Russian engineers always studied ship-building in England; Russians knew Shakespeare and Byron almost by heart; while the popularity of Dickens rivalled that of Dostoievsky and Leo Tolstoy. Especially surprising was the success enjoyed before the war by Wilde and Wells, whose works were endlessly being translated and published.
It is true, of course, that Russians who had never been in England were convinced that all Englishmen were tall and lean, all had red hair and all slept with pipes clenched between their teeth; while all Englishwomen had protruding teeth. Although even Dostoievsky wrote that if an Englishwoman is beautiful, her beauty cannot be surpassed, yet Russians were of the opinion that Englishwomen gave more thought to their archery than to their appearance. But in the year 1912, H. G. Wells arrived in Moscow for the first time, and said in a special article to "Russkoye Slovo," the most widely circulated newspaper in Russia, that nowhere in the world had he seen so many people resembling Englishmen as on the Kouznetsky Most in Moscow. The reign of King George V (Russians pronounce this name Ghe-org) was a period when Russia fell head over heels in love with everything English. This friendship was soon afterwards strengthened by the brotherhood of blood during the Great War. The news of Kitchener's death was received by Russians as if the loss was their own.
Russians were always especially impressed with the amazing resemblance between King George V and Czar Nicholas II. The story was constantly told how when he was young, King George, serving as a guest of his cousin, the Tsarevitch, visited St. Petersburg and was everywhere mistaken for the Czar. When King George died all Russian newspapers came out with a mourning border. The marriage of the Duke of Kent to Princess Marina, who is closely related to the Russian royal family, was also received with enthusiasm by Russians. The attitude of the
(b.s! Routed)
Russians toward the Coronation is readily understandable. Russian newspapers are issuing special Coronation numbers, and many Russian houses and shops will during the festivities be decorated with the British and Russian flags.
Marriage Season
The Easter holidays have ended and Red Hill, the marriage-season, has arrived. Easter has not only brought much joy in its wake, but has also proved very profitable to tradesmen. There were shops which on the day directly preceding Easter had sold all their merchandise. According to an approximate calculation, no less than $100,000 was spent by Russian Shanghai during the Easter holidays. The season of Easter festivities was concluded by a ball of the bohemian club "Khlam" in the Arcadia cabaret which was attended by unusual success.
Lectures and Debates
In reviewing the activities of the winter season must be mentioned the extraordinary success which Russian lectures and political debates have enjoyed, especially among the younger set. Lectures were given right through the winter in the Russian Club, in Sokol, in the Ex-Officers' Club, in the Russian Home in Wei-haiwei Road, in the Fascist Club and in the Union of the New Generation. Among the themes dealt with, the most popular were: "Russia To-day," "The Role of Emigration in the Future Russian Revolution," "Russia and China," "Admiral Makaroff" (one of the heroes of the siege of Port Arthur), "Will there be a War?" and others. In addition to those dealing with politics, scientific and literary themes were also popular. Archbishop Victor, the head of the Russian Orthodox Mission in China, gave a graphic account of his trip to Europe, when he attended the conference in Serbia of all Hierarchs outside of Russia.
There is in the Russian Colony a private Historical Society where, without any noise or publicity, a vast research work is being carried on. Political debates, especially in young people's clubs, bear a more stormy and a less academic character. Sometimes persons who have just escaped from the U.S.S.R. take part in these debates. Interest is evinced not only in what is happening in Russia, but also in fascism in Italy, in national-socialism in Germany, and in the civil war in Spain.
Gaols Visited
Following an old Russian custom, Bishop John, the head of the Orthodox churches in Shanghai, visited during the Easter holidays all gaols holding Russian prisoners, and all hospitals with Russian patients. These visits always bring joy to those imprisoned and those suffering from disease. Bishop John Khristosovula with oil, and for each and every one he found a word of comfort and encouragement.
10/5

作者：STROY

上海的俄国人正热切关注加冕庆典活动。俄国人始终记得，爱德华七世国王与亚历山大三世皇帝娶了两姐妹为妻。要判断导致两国在19世纪产生敌对、甚至引发克里米亚战争的原因并非易事，但自爱德华七世国王即位之初，俄国公众的善意便开始明确地转向英国。爱德华七世与尼古拉二世两位君主在雷瓦尔（Revel）的会晤，奠定了直至俄国帝制时代终结为止一直延续的友谊基础。就在几周前，俄国人饶有兴致地阅读了一篇历史随笔，文中讲述了大约100年前维多利亚女王与俄国皇储亚历山大·尼古拉耶维奇（即后来的沙皇亚历山大二世）之间迸发出的热烈友谊；当时这位皇储正为其父尼古拉一世皇帝出使伦敦。

尽管起初受法国文化影响，随后又受德国文化影响，但俄国人始终不仅珍视英国文化，也珍视英国文明。英国商品——布料、钢铁等——在俄国人眼中向来被视为最佳；俄国工程师总是在英国学习造船技术；俄国人几乎能背诵莎士比亚和拜伦的作品；而狄更斯的受欢迎程度可与陀思妥耶夫斯基和列夫·托尔斯泰相媲美。尤其令人惊讶的是，王尔德和威尔斯在战前享有的成功，他们的作品被无休止地翻译和出版。

诚然，那些从未去过英国的俄国人确信，所有英国人都身材高瘦，全是红头发，睡觉时嘴里都紧咬着烟斗；而所有英国女人都有龅牙。尽管连陀思妥耶夫斯基也曾写道，如果一位英国女子美丽，其美貌无可匹敌，但俄国人仍认为英国女子更注重射箭而非容貌。然而在1912年，H. G. 威尔斯首次抵达莫斯科，并在俄国发行量最大的报纸《俄罗斯言论报》（Russkoye Slovo）上发表专文称，他在世界上任何地方都没有像在莫斯科库兹涅茨基桥（Kouznetsky Most）那样见过如此多酷似英国人的人。乔治五世国王（俄国人将此名字发音为Ghe-org）在位时期，是俄国人对一切英国事物陷入狂热爱恋的时期。这种友谊不久后因大战期间的血肉同胞之情而得到加强。基钦纳勋爵去世的消息传来，俄国人感同身受，仿佛遭受了自身的损失。

俄国人始终对乔治五世国王与尼古拉二世沙皇之间惊人的相似之处印象深刻。人们常津津乐道这样一个故事：乔治国王年轻时作为表弟皇储的客人访问圣彼得堡，到处都被误认为是沙皇。乔治国王去世时，所有俄国报纸均刊出黑边以示哀悼。肯特公爵与玛丽娜公主的婚礼也受到俄国人的热烈欢迎，玛丽娜公主与俄国皇室关系密切。俄国人对加冕典礼的态度不难理解。俄国报纸正在发行加冕特刊，许多俄国住宅和商店将在庆典期间悬挂英国和俄国国旗。

婚嫁季节

复活节假期已结束，婚嫁旺季“红山节”（Red Hill）已经到来。复活节不仅带来了诸多欢乐，也被证明对商人非常有利。有些商店在复活节前一天就售光了所有商品。据粗略估算，上海俄界在复活节假期期间的花费不少于10万美元。复活节庆祝活动以波希米亚俱乐部“Khlam”在阿卡迪亚歌舞厅（Arcadia cabaret）举办的舞会落下帷幕，该舞会取得了异乎寻常的成功。

讲座与辩论

在回顾冬季活动时，必须提及俄国讲座和政治辩论取得的非凡成功，尤其是在年轻人群体中。整个冬季，讲座在俄国俱乐部、索科尔体育协会（Sokol）、退役军官俱乐部、威海卫路俄国之家、法西斯俱乐部以及新一代联盟等地举行。在所讨论的主题中，最受欢迎的包括：“今日的俄国”、“流亡者在未来俄国革命中的作用”、“俄国与中国”、“马卡洛夫海军上将”（旅顺口围困战中的英雄之一）、“会有战争吗？”等等。除了政治主题外，科学和文学主题也很受欢迎。中国东正教传教团团长维克多大主教生动地讲述了他前往欧洲的经历，当时他参加了在塞尔维亚举行的全俄境外主教会议。

俄国侨民区有一个私人历史学会，在不事张扬、没有公开宣传的情况下，正在进行大量的研究工作。政治辩论，特别是在青年俱乐部中，具有更为激烈且较少学术性的特点。有时，刚从苏联逃脱的人也会参加这些辩论。人们不仅对俄国国内发生的事情感兴趣，也对意大利的法西斯主义、德国的国家社会主义以及西班牙的内战表现出兴趣。

探访监狱

遵循一项古老的俄国习俗，上海东正教会主教约翰在复活节假期期间探访了所有关押俄国囚犯的监狱，以及所有收治俄国病人的医院。这些探访总是给身陷囹圄者和患病者带来欢乐。约翰主教用圣油为他们施涂圣礼，并为每一个人找到了安慰和鼓励的话语。
10/5

NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, MONDAY, MAY 17, 1937
218691
REV.
B. D. 5002
20 5 37

IN THE
RUSSIAN
COLONY

By Smox

There is an interesting custom characterizing Russian religion of which foreigners know almost nothing. Last Tuesday was Radonitza. This briefly is a service for the dead held over their graves. Following this custom—which extends as far back as pagan antiquity, when ancient Russians were fond of feasting on the graves of the newly-buried—All, young and old, on the Tuesday of the week following Pascha go to the cemeteries where the graves of those dear to them are interred. They take with them everything left over from the abundant Easter table: kulichi which had time to become somewhat stale, paskas, coloured eggs —they even take vodka. First they prepare a special dish in commemoration of the dead called kutia, which actually is nothing more than boiled rice mixed with sugar and raisins and decorated with sweets made of marmalade. When on this day the priest holds a short requiem service over the graves of relatives, a small wax candle is struck into the kutia, and burns while the sacred words of the prayer are being pronounced. On this day priests will, on being invited by the faithful, go from grave to grave, holding services over each one.

When the religious ceremony is over the candle on the kutia is snuffed and all, starting with the priest and followed by the relatives of the person in the grave, sample the kutia with a little spoon. What is left over is given to the poor who on this day are always numerous in cemeteries. At the end of the service the common people often remain behind on the graves; small benches are united, various delicacies appear, and, following the example set by the ancient Slavs, who celebrated trizna, they eat and drink to the memory of whoever is buried below them.

Shanghai Remembers

In Shanghai, of course, Radonitza has lost much of its colourfulness. Here there is no one main Russian cemetery with a Russian church (as in Harbin) where on a Spring day crowds drift with their little bundles. Here there are no long rows of marked Russian burials with fences around them, two-sided along the alley leading to the church. Here no parts are held over graves in memory of the dead—here all that Russians do on this day is go to the cemeteries and hold a short mass. This was done last Tuesday in Bubbling Well Cemetery, where there is a common grave for the Russian soldiers and officers who during the Russo-Japanese war died in Shanghai, and where in the section nearest Avenue Foch there are already many graves of well-known and respected Russian residents of the past. In Bubbling Well Cemetery; in the cemetery at Lo Ya Wei, where the number of Russian graves exceeds the number of non-Russian ones, and finally in Ziccawei Cemetery where the poorest, often destitute Russians are buried. The priests of all Russian churches were gathered in the Bubbling Well and Bubbling John, after conducting the service over the soldiers' common grave in Bubbling Well, went to Ziccawei for an especially sad visit to the cemetery of the poor in Ziccawei.

All through the day cemeteries were filled with Russians. Russians have a profound feeling for the sacred beauty of Death. A Russian is dead. Women (necessarily women) make the final ablutions of the body, for it is a woman who brings a human being to life, and her hands must therefore wash him and put him to rest. A nun is summoned to the coffin and reads continuously (especially at night) the psalms of David, the favourite book of the Russians. The church sends to the house of the dead a pall of gold brocade, a special heavy kind of material which is worn by the priests only during the service. The dead body in the coffin is covered by this sacred cloth, as by a priestly chasuble. Tall waxen candles are kept burning by the side of the coffin in silver candlesticks of peculiar form, also sent from the church. No ordinary candlesticks can be used for this purpose. Three candles are burned, and their light and the reading of the Psalms make it appear, especially at night, that a temporary church has been created around the departed.

SORO Meeting

A general meeting of the representatives of all organizations which form SORO was held recently. Mr. Tsao, representative of the local branch of the Kuomintang, was also present. Gen. F. L. Gleboff, the chairman of SORO, noted in his address that up to March 1, 1937, SORO had registered 15,583 emigrants and issued 7,406 documents. It was unanimously agreed that the present board of the SORO should continue up to March 1, 1938. The association thanked the Chinese authorities, in the person of Mr. Tsao, for their attentive attitude toward the needs of Russian emigrants.

Women's School

In the Ladies' Professional School, which was founded five years ago by "The Shanghai Zaria" and which later came under the direction of the French authorities, Spring examinations have just begun. Those in cutting, sewing and manicuring have already been held, and examinations on every other specialized subject taught in the school are to follow. So far sixteen women and girls have graduated from this school this year. There is a plan to open in the near future a special European dressmakers' shop where those for whom the fashionable shops are too expensive, but who do not like to use cheap Chinese tailors, can make their dresses. The small number of Russian dressmakers' assistants in local salons employed at the present time is explained by the fact that up till now there have been few women and girls with sufficient knowledge and the necessary qualifications in this field. It is the aim of the Ladies' Professional School to fill this deficiency.

Artist Leaves

Last Saturday Mr. J. Rakofieff, an artist who is well known in Russian and Russian circles, left for Peking where he will make paintings of temples and palaces. In preparation for his large exhibition (exhibition of Landscapes & Architecture) in the building of the Russian Club.

(bel Rakofieff)

《字林西报》，1937年5月17日，星期一
218691
REV.
B. D. 5002
1937年5月20日

在
俄国
侨民区

作者：Smox

有一种体现俄国宗教特色的有趣习俗，外国人几乎一无所知。上周二是拉多尼察节（Radonitza）。简而言之，这是一种在死者墓前举行的祭奠仪式。遵循这一习俗——其渊源可追溯至异教古代，当时古俄人喜欢在刚下葬者的墓前宴饮——在复活节（Pascha）后那一周的星期二，无论老少，都会前往安葬着他们亲人的墓地。他们会带上丰盛的复活节餐桌上剩余的所有食物：已经有些变硬的库利奇面包（kulichi）、帕斯卡奶酪蛋糕（paskas）、彩蛋——他们甚至带上伏特加酒。首先，他们会准备一种纪念死者的特色菜肴，称为库季亚（kutia），这实际上不过是拌有糖和葡萄干的煮米饭，并用果脯制成的糖果加以装饰。当这一天神父在亲属墓前举行简短的安魂弥撒时，一支小蜡烛会被插在库季亚中，并在诵读神圣祷文期间一直燃烧。在这一天，应信徒邀请，神父们会逐墓巡视，为每一座坟墓举行仪式。

宗教仪式结束后，库季亚上的蜡烛被熄灭，从神父开始，随后是逝者的亲属，所有人都用小勺品尝库季亚。剩余的食物会分给穷人，这一天墓地里总是聚集着许多穷人。仪式结束后，平民百姓常常留在墓地上；他们将小长凳拼在一起，摆出各种美味佳肴，效仿庆祝特里兹纳祭（trizna）的古斯拉夫人的榜样，吃喝以纪念埋葬在他们脚下的人。

上海的记忆

当然，在上海，拉多尼察节已失去了许多色彩。这里没有像哈尔滨那样拥有一座带俄国教堂的主要俄国公墓，在春日里人群带着小包裹缓缓流向那里。这里没有沿着通往教堂的小径两侧排列的、围有栅栏的成排标记清晰的俄国墓葬。这里不在墓前举行纪念死者的聚会——在这里，俄国人在这天所做的只是前往墓地并举行一场简短的弥撒。上周二在静安寺公墓（Bubbling Well Cemetery）就是这样做的，那里有一处合葬墓，安葬着在日俄战争期间死于上海的俄国士兵和军官，而在靠近福煦路（Avenue Foch）的区域，已有许多过去知名且受尊敬的俄国居民的坟墓。在静安寺公墓；在罗家威（Lo Ya Wei，音译）公墓，那里的俄国坟墓数量超过了非俄国人的坟墓数量；最后是在徐家汇（Ziccawei）公墓，那里安葬着最贫穷、往往是一无所有的俄国人。所有俄国教堂的神父都聚集在静安寺，在静安寺的士兵合葬墓举行仪式后，前往徐家汇，对徐家汇的穷人公墓进行了一次特别令人伤感的探访。

整天墓地里都挤满了俄国人。俄国人对于死亡的神圣之美有着深刻的感受。俄国人去世了。女性（必须是女性）为遗体进行最后的净身，因为是女人将人带到世间，因此必须由她的双手为他清洗并让他安息。一位修女被召到棺木旁，不间断地（尤其是在夜间）诵读大卫诗篇，这是俄国人最喜爱的书籍。教堂向死者家中送去一块金锦缎制成的尸衣，这是一种特殊的厚重面料，仅在仪式期间由神父穿戴。棺中的遗体被这块神圣的布料覆盖，如同披上神父的法衣。高大的蜡烛在棺材旁燃烧，插在形状奇特的银烛台中，这些烛台也是从教堂送来的。普通的烛台不能用于此目的。点燃三支蜡烛，烛光与诗篇的诵读声营造出一种氛围，尤其在夜间，仿佛围绕逝者建立了一座临时教堂。

SORO会议

最近举行了组成SORO的各组织代表联席会议。国民党当地分支的代表曹先生（Mr. Tsao，音译）也出席了会议。SORO主席格列博夫将军（Gen. F. L. Gleboff）在讲话中指出，截至1937年3月1日，SORO已登记移民15,583人，并发放了7,406份文件。会议一致同意现任SORO董事会任期延续至1938年3月1日。该协会通过曹先生感谢中国当局对俄国移民需求的关注态度。

女子职业学校

由“上海扎里亚”（The Shanghai Zaria）五年前创办、后来归法国当局管理的女子职业学校，春季考试刚刚开始。裁剪、缝纫和美甲科目的考试已经举行，学校教授的其他专业科目的考试也将陆续进行。今年迄今已有16名妇女和女孩从该校毕业。计划在不久的将来开设一家专门的欧式裁缝店，供那些觉得时尚商店太贵、但又不喜欢使用廉价中国裁缝的人制作服装。目前本地沙龙中聘用的俄国裁缝助手数量稀少，原因在于迄今为止在该领域拥有足够知识和必要资格的妇女和女孩寥寥无几。女子职业学校的目标正是弥补这一不足。

艺术家离沪

上周六，在俄国及俄裔圈子里颇有名气的艺术家J. Rakofieff先生（音译）启程前往北平，他将在那里绘制寺庙和宫殿的画作。这是为他即将在俄国俱乐部大楼举办的大型展览（风景与建筑展）做准备。

(bel Rakofieff)
