THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, MONDAY, APRIL 26, 1937

IN THE
RUSSIAN
COLONY

By STROY

Last Sunday was Verbnolé (Palm)
Sunday. It was preceded by Verb-
naia Saturday, or St. Lazarus' Day,
when the Russian Church recalls
the resurrection of Lazarus and the
entry of Christ into Jerusalem.

In bleak, northern Russia there
are no palms; and so the symbol by
which these Biblical happenings
were recalled became the verba, or
sallow (Salix Alba) (a shrub closely
akin to the willow) which is the
first to awaken after the prolonged
and raw Russian winter. The long
twigs of the verba, the small, grey-
ish-white, silken buds of this northern
plant, so fragrant with the freshness
of spring, to Russians signify the be-
ginning of the week of Our Saviour's
Passion.

All Orthodox churches were last
Saturday richly decorated with the
Shanghai substitutes of verba. All
congregations held thin lighted
candles and faggots of shrub in
their hands. Three times this week
Russians stand all through the pre-
Easter services holding lighted
candles: on St. Lazarus' Saturday
which has already passed, on Great
Thursday, when twelve chosen chap-
ters will be read out of the Gospel,
and at midnight on Saturday next,
during the Zautrenia, when for Rus-
sians their long-awaited Easter will
finally arrive.

The spectacle presented by
churches at this time—filled, as they
are, with worshippers all holding
candles in their hands—is of sur-
prising beauty. Candles are not
blown out when the service ends
but they are carried home with the
flames still alive. Thus, when the
congregation turns homeward from
the church, carefully shielding their
burning candles with their hands,
each candle like a glow-worm in the
night—the whole forms a fairy-like
picture. It is the custom on such
occasions to hit gently and lovingly
friends and acquaintances with the
"verbas especially those sleepy in
the early hours of the morning, say-
ing "I'm not hitting you—the verba
is!" or "Don't blame the verba;
blame your old sins," or, again,
"Verba krasna, biet naprasno; verba
biela biet za dielo."—an untranslat-
able play on words, something to
the effect of "verba hits un-
reasoningly; white verba hits with
purpose."

Charity Work

In old Russia, before the war and
the revolution, St. Lazarus' Satur-
day played an important part in
the world of charity. Every-where
charity bazaars were held, and the
large proceeds of such bazaars went
to the destitute and unfortunate.
In St. Petersburg, the Empress per-
sonally opened the largest and grand-
est bazaar in all Russia. In addi-
tion to the various articles and toys
which, during the first day of Easter,
were given out freely to the chil-
dren, these bazaars sold the verba,
several twigs with buds already
opened artistically arranged adorned
with artificial flowers and inter-
twined with silk ribbons. In the
streets, in imitation of older this
solemn custom of carrying the sacred
boughs from churches became gener-
ally among the younger. Each had a
merry expression, with everyone say-
ing to his neighbour this: the old
angry way, and it, defeats the rule.

Verbnaia Saturday is the last day
when one is allowed to smile openly.
When on Thursday evening Russians
wend their way home from church,
their faces will be set in a stern
expression. On this Thursday, it is
necessary at all costs reach home
with the candle still burning, and
with its flame make the sign of the
cross in the doorway. Russians will
once more start to smile and enjoy
themselves only a week hence—on
Easter, after the Zautrenia, when
everyone can kiss everyone else
three time (christosovatsa) where-
ever they meet—even in the street.

Former Judge Arrives

Prof. C. F. Kichin, one of the
oldest judicial authorities of pre-
revolution Russia, has arrived here
from Harbin. Before the revolution
he occupied the post of procurator
in the district court at Orenburg,
and later became president of the
court at Vladivostok. When an in-
dependent White Government was
set up in the Maritime Provinces
with Mr. S. D. Merkuloff as chair-
man, Mr. Kitchin was elected Minis-
ter of Justice. He held this post
right up to the time when the White
Army was evacuated by Gen. M. K.
Diterichs to Korea and China. In
emigration, Mr. Kichin devoted him-
self wholly to the teaching pro-
fession, and has long held the post
of Professor of Law in the Law
College of Harbin. This Law Col-
lege was founded seventeen years
ago by Russian scholars who were
forced by the revolution to leave
their country. In it scores of young
men—Chinese as well as Russian—
have received their training in law;
and many of them to-day hold im-
portant positions in China. It is
interesting to note that Mr. Li Shao-
ken, former president of the Board
of the Chinese Eastern Railway, and
at present Minister of Communica-
tions of Manchukuo, graduated from
this college. It is feared that with
the present altered conditions in
Harbin, this institution will be forced
to close its doors.

Handicraft Exhibition

An exhibition of handicraft has
been opened at the Russian Club.
Among the contributors to this ex-
hibition are representatives of every
circle in the colony: society ladies,
convent nuns, and girl-pupils of
the St. Andrew's Preparatory School.
Many of the articles displayed are
works of true artistry.

Dostoievsky Evening

At the Social Club an evening was
devoted to the memory of the famous
Russian author and philosopher, F. M.
Dostoievsky. An account of his life
and works was given by the chair-
man of the Literary Section,
Mr. B. A. Tchernavin, who also
read some extracts from his works.
The evening concluded with a dis-
cussion on the psychological aspects
of Dostoievsky's writings, in which
many members took part. The even-
ing was well attended, and much
interest was shown in the subject.
page_data.zh:
《字林西报》，1937年4月26日，星期一

在
俄国
侨民区

作者：STROY

上周日是柳枝主日（Verbnolé，即棕榈主日）。此前是柳枝星期六（Verbnaia Saturday），或称圣拉撒路日（St. Lazarus' Day），俄国教会在此日纪念拉撒路的复活以及基督进入耶路撒冷。

在荒凉的俄罗斯北部没有棕榈树；因此，用来纪念这些圣经事件的象征物变成了“verba”，即白柳（Salix Alba）（一种与柳树非常相近的灌木），它是漫长而阴冷的俄罗斯冬季过后最先苏醒的植物。这种北方植物长长的枝条，灰白色丝绒般的小芽，散发着春天的清新气息，对俄国人而言，标志着救世主受难周的开始。

上周六，所有东正教教堂都用上海产的“verba”替代品装饰得富丽堂皇。所有会众手中都拿着点燃的细蜡烛和一束束灌木枝条。在这一周里，俄国人要在整个复活节前礼拜期间手持点燃的蜡烛站立三次：在已经过去的圣拉撒路星期六；在圣周四，届时将从福音书中诵读选定的十二章；以及在下周六午夜的晨祷（Zautrenia）期间，对俄国人来说，他们期盼已久的复活节终于到来。

此时教堂呈现的景象——挤满了手持蜡烛的信徒——具有惊人的美感。仪式结束时蜡烛并不吹灭，而是让火焰继续燃烧着带回家。因此，当会众从教堂回家时，小心翼翼地用手护着燃烧的蜡烛，每支蜡烛都像夜间的萤火虫——整体构成了一幅如童话般的画面。在这种场合，习惯是用“verba”轻轻且充满爱意地拍打朋友和熟人，尤其是那些清晨昏昏欲睡的人，说着：“不是我打你，是verba在打！”或者“别怪verba，怪你的旧罪孽，”又或者，“Verba krasna, biet naprasno; verba biela biet za dielo.”——这是一句无法翻译的文字游戏，大意是“红色的verba无理地打；白色的verba有目的地打。”

慈善工作

在战前和革命前的旧俄国，圣拉撒路星期六在慈善界扮演着重要角色。各地都举行慈善义卖会，义卖会的巨额收益用于帮助贫困和不幸的人。在圣彼得堡，皇后亲自全俄最大、最宏伟的义卖会开幕。除了在复活节第一天免费发放给儿童的各种物品和玩具外，这些义卖会还出售“verba”，几根带有已绽放花蕾的枝条经过艺术排列，饰以人造花朵并交织着丝带。在街道上，模仿这一古老习俗，年轻人中普遍流行从教堂携带神圣枝条的做法。每个人都面带愉快的表情，每个人都对邻居这样说：那种古老的愤怒方式，以及它，违背了规则。（注：此处原文逻辑混乱，似有OCR错误或原文表述不清，照实译出）

柳枝星期六是允许公开微笑的最后一天。当周四晚上俄国人从教堂走回家时，他们的脸上将呈现出严肃的表情。在这个周四，无论如何必须让蜡烛保持燃烧到家，并用其火焰在门口画十字。俄国人要再过一周才会再次开始微笑和享乐——即在复活节，晨祷之后，那时无论在哪里相遇——甚至在街上——每个人都可以亲吻其他人三次（christosovatsa，互祝基督复活）。

前法官抵沪

C. F. Kichin教授（音译），革命前俄国最资深的司法权威之一，已从哈尔滨抵达此地。革命前，他担任奥伦堡地区法院的检察官，后来成为符拉迪沃斯托克法院院长。当滨海边疆区成立独立的白军政府，由S. D. Merkuloff先生（音译）担任主席时，Kitchin先生当选为司法部长。他一直担任此职，直到白军由M. K. Diterichs将军（音译）撤离至朝鲜和中国。流亡期间，Kichin先生全心投入教育事业，长期担任哈尔滨法学院法学教授。该法学院由十七年前因革命被迫离开祖国的俄国学者创立。数十名年轻人——包括中国人和俄国人——在此接受法律培训；其中许多人今天在中国担任重要职务。值得注意的是，前中东铁路理事会理事长、现任伪满洲国交通大臣的李绍肯先生（Li Shao-ken，音译）毕业于该学院。令人担忧的是，鉴于哈尔滨目前的局势变化，该机构将被迫关闭。

手工艺品展览

俄国俱乐部举办了一场手工艺品展览。参展者包括侨民界各阶层的代表：社交界女士、修道院修女以及圣安德烈预备学校的女学生。许多展出的作品堪称真正的艺术佳作。

陀思妥耶夫斯基之夜

在社交俱乐部，举办了一个纪念著名俄国作家和哲学家F. M. 陀思妥耶夫斯基的夜晚。文学组主席B. A. Tchernavin先生（音译）介绍了他的生平和作品，并朗读了其作品的一些摘录。晚会最后进行了关于陀思妥耶夫斯基著作心理层面的讨论，许多成员参与其中。晚会出席人数众多，大家对这一主题表现出浓厚兴趣。

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, MONDAY, APRIL 12, 1937

IN THE
RUSSIAN
COLONY

By Smov

Exactly fifteen years had elapsed last week since the Harbin Polytechnic Institute was founded with the energetic help of Mr. B. V. Ostromoff, then General Manager of the Chinese Eastern Railway. In Shanghai there are at present no less than 100 young Russian engineers graduated from that institute; and nearly all of these have found work in their line. In the years 1930—1933 when many buildings were being erected in the city, Russian architects found wide use for the work in which they specialized. A young Russian architect was employed in the construction of almost every building, and firms like Palmer & Turner; Davies, Brook and Gran; and Corritt & Co. readily gave work to Russians. Mechanical and electrical engineers, however, found work with great difficulty. To-day the situation has changed: electro-mechanics are hired much more readily than architects because of the continuous depression in the land and building market.

As a rule, Russian engineers work for a smaller salary than other foreigners, although there are at present three or four men who have reached a position where their labour is assessed just as high. Last year began a migration towards the south. Several former graduates of the Harbin Polytechnic Institute are at present employed in Hongkong, Canton and the Philippines. The average monthly earnings of the young Russian engineer in Shanghai range between $150 and $200. The majority of these youthful engineers are members of the Russian Technical Society. On the fifteenth anniversary of the founding of their alma-mater they held an anniversary dinner at which many appropriate speeches were given.

Professor Dies

The death occurred last week of Prof. N. D. Mironoff, who for nearly ten years has lived in Shanghai. In one month, Russian science in the Far East has lost two worthy scholars—the Baron Von Stahl, who died in Peiping, and Prof. Mironoff. It is a strange coincidence that both were authorities in Sanskrit. In addition they had a finest knowledge of many other languages. Before the revolution, Prof. Mironoff worked in the Imperial Academy of Sciences, and in the days of the provisional government was the director of the press bureau in St. Petersburg. He came to Shanghai on the invitation of the famous Japanese buddhist, Count Otani, to decipher and arrange certain manuscripts found in the caves of the ancient Buddhist temples in Central Asia. In addition to that, Prof. Mironoff was for some time a member of the staff of the First Russian School.

National Committee

A meeting of the representatives of all the organizations which are part of the National Committee was held recently at the offices of the Russian Club in Avenue Foch. The agenda included reports on the activities of the various sections and the election of new officers. It was decided to hold a general assembly of the Russian colony in the near future to discuss matters of common interest.

Boy Scouts

In Shanghai recently the National Organization of Russian Boy Scouts (Rasvedchiki), has been started. This organization is patronized by H.I.H. the Grand Duchess Xenia. After a service in the Russian Cathedral, the ceremony of presenting the colours was held. On the banner is depicted the image of St. Nicholas, the monogram of Emperor Peter the Great, and—in ancient Slavic letters—the motto: "With Us Into Battle For Russia." Several hundred boys between the ages of ten and seventeen are members of this organization, which is directed by Col. N. G. Yakovlev.

New Plays

The Russian theatre has in emigration always suffered from a lack of suitable plays. Plays written before the revolution have become obsolete; Soviet plays still contain much propaganda—consequently the plays of ancient Russian classical writers have had to be staged too often. Now this defect is disappearing as more and more plays are being written by emigrant-playwrights. In Paris such celebrities as Aldamov, Surgucheff and others write for the Russian Theatre, while in Shanghai there will be produced in the near future a play entitled, "The Woman They Never Mention," written by Mrs. L. N. Kniajevitch.

This is the story of a Russian woman in Shanghai who is forced by circumstances to face life alone. Her husband is a former officer who fought in the Civil War, served in the Chinese Army, took to drink and descended in life. Her daughter lives in a foreign convent in another city, as her mother does not wish her to see the way in which she lives. Finishing school, the daughter unexpectedly comes to visit her stranger-mother. The play will undoubtedly create wide discussion in the colony, and, in fact, already has, as Mrs. Kniajevitch read it in the literary club Monday.

Club Sports Section

The Russian Club in Avenue Foch has opened a sports section for members and their children, and an open-air gymnasium has been constructed in the Club garden. The director of this section will be Mr. Buyantover. The Club often organizes dances which are popular among the younger set. Sports teams will play against those of the British Club and others in the city. On April 18, Russian sportsmen are holding a cross-country race for which many prizes will be distributed.

Cross Raised

Yesterday was a day of great moment in the Russian colony. The large gilded cross, which until then was kept in the Russian Cathedral, was erected on the main cupola of that church. Many of the colony were present at the ceremony. Every Orthodox church in Shanghai took part in the service. The new cross will be illuminated at night.

《字林西报》，1937年4月12日，星期一

在
俄国
侨民区

作者：Smov

上周恰是哈尔滨工业大学在时任中东铁路总经理B. V. Ostromoff先生的大力协助下成立十五周年。目前在上海，毕业于该学院的年轻俄国工程师不少于100人；且几乎所有人都已找到对口工作。在1930至1933年间，随着城市中许多建筑拔地而起，俄国建筑师在其专业领域内获得了广泛的工作机会。几乎每座建筑的施工中都有年轻的俄国建筑师受聘，像公和洋行（Palmer & Turner）、戴维斯·布鲁克与格兰公司（Davies, Brook and Gran）以及科里特公司（Corritt & Co.）等商行都乐于雇佣俄国人。然而，机械和电气工程师找工作却极为困难。如今情况已发生变化：由于土地和建筑市场持续萧条，机电工程师比建筑师更容易被雇佣。

通常，俄国工程师的薪水低于其他外籍人士，尽管目前有三四人已达到其劳动价值被评估为同等高水平的地位。去年开始了向南迁移的趋势。几位前哈尔滨工业大学的毕业生目前受雇于香港、广州和菲律宾。在上海的年轻俄国工程师平均月收入在150至200元之间。这些年轻工程师大多数是俄国技术学会的成员。在校庆十五周年之际，他们举行了纪念晚宴，会上发表了许多得体的演讲。

Dies教授

N. D. Mironoff教授于上周逝世，他在上海生活了近十年。在一个月内，远东的俄国科学界失去了两位值得尊敬的学者——在北平逝世的冯·施塔尔男爵（Baron Von Stahl）和Mironoff教授。奇怪的是，两人都是梵文领域的权威。此外，他们还精通许多其他语言。革命前，Mironoff教授在帝国科学院工作，在临时政府时期担任圣彼得堡新闻局局长。他应著名日本佛教徒大谷伯爵（Count Otani）的邀请来到上海，对在中亚古佛教寺庙洞穴中发现的一些手稿进行破译和整理。此外，Mironoff教授曾一度在第一俄国学校任职。

全国委员会

最近，属于全国委员会的各组织代表在霞飞路（Avenue Foch）俄国俱乐部办公室举行了一次会议。议程包括各部门活动报告和新职员选举。会议决定在不久的将来举行俄国侨民大会，讨论共同关心的问题。

童子军

最近，俄国童子军国家组织（Rasvedchiki）在上海成立。该组织由谢尼娅女大公殿下（H.I.H. the Grand Duchess Xenia）赞助。在俄国大教堂举行礼拜仪式后，举行了授旗仪式。旗帜上绘有圣尼古拉的画像、彼得大帝皇帝的花押字，以及用古斯拉夫字母书写的格言：“与我们一起为俄罗斯而战”。该组织拥有数百名年龄在十至十七岁之间的男孩，由N. G. Yakovlev上校领导。

新剧目

俄国剧院在流亡期间一直苦于缺乏合适的剧本。革命前创作的剧本已过时；苏联剧本仍包含大量宣传内容——因此，不得不频繁上演古代俄国古典作家的剧目。现在这一缺陷正在消失，因为越来越多的流亡剧作家正在创作剧本。在巴黎，Aldamov、Surgucheff等名家为俄国剧院写作，而在上海，不久将上演L. N. Kniajevitch夫人创作的剧本《他们从未提及的女人》（The Woman They Never Mention）。

该剧讲述了一位在上海的俄国妇女因环境所迫独自面对生活的故事。她的丈夫是一名曾在内战中作战、后在中国军队服役的前军官，因酗酒而生活堕落。她的女儿住在另一座城市的外国修道院里，因为母亲不希望女儿看到自己的生活状况。女儿毕业后，意外前来探望这位形同陌路的母亲。该剧无疑将在侨民区引起广泛讨论，事实上讨论已经开始，因为Kniajevitch夫人已于周一在文学俱乐部朗读了该剧。

俱乐部体育部

霞飞路俄国俱乐部已为会员及其子女开设体育部，并在俱乐部花园内建造了一个露天健身房。该部主任由Buyantover先生担任。俱乐部经常举办舞会，深受年轻人欢迎。运动队将与英国俱乐部及市内其他俱乐部的队伍进行比赛。4月18日，俄国运动员将举行越野赛跑，届时将颁发许多奖项。

十字架竖起

昨天是俄国侨民区具有重大意义的日子。此前一直保存在俄国大教堂内的巨大镀金十字架，被竖立在该教堂的主圆顶上。许多侨民出席了仪式。上海所有的东正教教堂都参与了礼拜。新十字架将在夜间点亮。

page_data.en:
THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, MONDAY, APRIL 5, 1937

IN THE
RUSSIAN
COLONY

By STROY

Every foreign school in Shanghai has its quota of Russian pupils. In the Public and Thomas Hanbury School, and the College Municipal Français they are especially numerous. In addition, there are now Russian students in St. John's University, in the Henry Lester Institute, in the University of Shanghai, and in L'Universite de l'Aurore.

Notwithstanding this large number of Russians in foreign schools, the number in Russian schools is still larger, closely approaching 600. These are distributed among—the Commercial School in Avenue Petain, the First Russian School in Yulin Road, the Girls' High School in the same building as the Russian Women's League, and St. Andrew's Primary School. Recently the French authorities built and equipped generously the Ecole Remi building, where at present 300 pupils—all Russians—receive their education. Many French members of the staff—among them the principal, M. Nicolet de Cholet, speak fluent Russian. This week another school, the Russian High School, will be opened at 89 MacGregor Road under the able leadership of Mr. I. N. Sofonoff and his assistant, Mr. N. K. Ivanoff.

Thus, in spite of the competition offered by the better equipped foreign institutions, Russian schools not only exist but are increasing in number. This is explained by the fact that many Russian parents insist upon their children receiving at least their middle-school education in Russian schools. They are alarmed by the process of denationalization which is evidenced not only in Shanghai but wherever Russian emigration has penetrated.

There are already many young men and women who, from childhood educated in foreign schools, to-day speak their mother tongue infinitely worse than English. Even if they do still speak Russian, they cannot write well, seldom read Russian classics, and Russian newspapers and journals almost never. At home they speak English among themselves, so that parents often do not know what their children talk about at table. All this makes Russian parents give their support to Russian schools and educate their children there, taking the risk that upon graduating they will find it harder to find jobs than those finishing foreign schools. This tendency is especially strong in families who have not surrendered the dream of returning to their homeland at the first opportunity.

Again, parents who educate their sons and daughters in Russian schools reason thus: Shanghai is not France or America, where on learning the language and becoming naturalised one can cease being Russian. In Shanghai an emigrant will always remain an emigrant; and in spite of its cosmopolitan character, this great metropolis is divided into colonies, and each colony lives, after all, its own life. Mouth which breaks away from the Russian colony cannot wholly unite itself with any other.

Registration

On March 9, the Standing Committee of the local branch of the Kuomintang passed Resolution No. 2767, which, in reply to the petition filed by the United Russian Association (SORO), approved the registration of this organization. The Appealing Committee of the local Kuomintang insisted that the SORO regulate its activities in line with the regulations of the Kuomintang, and that in all cases make reports to the Kuomintang without delay. In publicizing this statement, the Chairman of SORO, General F. L. Gleboff, asks Russians not to miss the date of registration of their passports, as that would result in fines and sometimes, in Chinese territory, in detention. The same work as that done by the SORO is carried out by the Russian Emigrants' Committee in Moulmein Road, whose Chairman, Mr. Ch. Metzler, is at the same time the representative of the Russian Community.

Cossack Holiday

On March 30, (St. Alexis' Day) Cossacks of the Russian Far East celebrated their holiday. Prayers were held in the Russian Cathedral —the church being filled with worshippers—after which tea was served in the premises of the Cossack Union. Among those present were Colonel D. V. Kochnev, Chairman of the Cossack Union, General V. V. Zimin, Chairman of the Union of War Invalids, General P. P. Oglobin and many others. A telegram of congratulation was received from the Ataman of all Cossacks in the Far East— G. M. Semionoff, residing in Dairen.

Aviator in Shanghai

Mr. P. E. Homiakoff arrived on March 31. Mr. Homiakoff, who is in charge of aviation in the port of Tsingtao, flew to Shanghai in order to acquaint himself with the two new aircraft which have been sent here from the Sikorsky factory in the United States. During the Great War Mr. Homiakoff worked in Russia with Sikorsky.

Interesting Lecture

Mr. A. M. Kolenev, the well-known jurist and author of the book "New Lamps for Old," gave an interesting lecture in the ex-Officers' Club on "The Boxer Uprising According to the Latest Investigations." Mr. Kotenev recently completed his new book "Soldier of China," which, will be published in Chinese as well as in other languages. He has collected rich material on the martial history of China from ancient times up to the present day.

Corps Anniversary

Last Thursday an anniversary dinner was held in the French Police Club in celebration of the fifth anniversary of the forming of the Russian Detachment. Headed by the Director of the Police, Commandant L. Fabre, the dinner was attended by all the officers of the corps, and also by the highest ranks of the French police and many representatives of the Municipalité Française. In a brilliant speech to the Russian Detachment, M. Fabre said that ever since its formation by General F. L. Gleboff during the 1931 troubles, men and officers alike have always showed a high sense of duty and honour. In all their five years of service, there was not one misunderstanding, not one unfavourable report, not one need for reproof. At the end of his speech everyone stood up while M. Fabre read the names of all Russian officers and men who were awarded gold and bronze medals for valour; some of them M. Fabre pointed out, met death when fulfilling their duty.

《字林西报》，1937年4月5日，星期一

在
俄国
侨民区

作者：STROY

上海的每一所外籍学校都有一定数量的俄国学生。在公共租界工部局学校、托马斯·汉伯里学校（Thomas Hanbury School）以及法公董局学校（College Municipal Français），俄国学生尤其众多。此外，圣约翰大学、雷士德工学院（Henry Lester Institute）、沪江大学（University of Shanghai）和震旦大学（L'Universite de l'Aurore）目前也有俄国学生。

尽管在外籍学校就读的俄国人数众多，但在俄国学校就读的人数仍然更多，接近600人。这些学生分布在——贝当路（Avenue Petain）的商业学校、榆林路的第一俄国学校、与俄国妇女联盟同在一栋楼的女子中学，以及圣安德鲁小学。最近，法国当局慷慨资助建设并装备了雷米学校（Ecole Remi）校舍，目前该校有300名学生——全是俄国人——在此接受教育。许多法籍教职员——其中包括校长Nicolet de Cholet先生——都能说流利的俄语。本周，另一所学校，即俄国中学，将在麦格雷戈路（MacGregor Road）89号开学，由I. N. Sofonoff先生及其助手N. K. Ivanoff先生能干地领导。

因此，尽管面临设备更精良的外籍机构的竞争，俄国学校不仅存在，而且数量还在增加。这是因为许多俄国父母坚持让孩子至少在中学阶段接受俄国学校的教育。他们对去俄国化过程感到震惊，这种现象不仅在上海，而且在俄国移民渗透到的任何地方都有体现。

已经有许多年轻男女，从小在外籍学校受教育，如今讲母语的能力远不如英语。即使他们仍会说俄语，也写不好，很少阅读俄国经典著作，几乎从不阅读俄国报纸和期刊。在家里他们用英语交谈，以至于父母往往不知道孩子们在餐桌上谈论什么。所有这些都促使俄国父母支持俄国学校，并将孩子送到那里受教育，哪怕冒着毕业后比外籍学校毕业生更难找工作的风险。这种倾向在那些尚未放弃一旦有机会就返回祖国梦想的家庭中尤为强烈。

此外，让子女在俄国学校受教育的父母这样推理：上海不是法国或美国，在那里学会语言并入籍后就可以不再做俄国人。在上海，移民将永远是移民；尽管这座大都市具有世界性特征，但它仍划分为各个侨民区，每个侨民区终究过着自己的生活。脱离俄国侨民区的人无法完全融入任何其他群体。

登记

3月9日，国民党当地支部常务委员会通过了第2767号决议，回应全俄联合会（SORO）提交的请愿书，批准该组织的登记。国民党当地支部上诉委员会坚持要求SORO按照国民党的规定规范其活动，并在所有情况下立即向国民党报告。在公布这一声明时，SORO主席F. L. Gleboff将军呼吁俄国人不要错过护照登记的日期，否则会导致罚款，有时在中国领土上还会导致拘留。穆尔门路（Moulmein Road）的俄国移民委员会也在开展与SORO相同的工作，其主席Ch. Metzler先生同时也是俄国社区的代表。

哥萨克节日

3月30日（圣阿列克谢日），远东俄国哥萨克人庆祝了他们的节日。在俄国大教堂举行了祈祷仪式——教堂里挤满了信徒——随后在哥萨克联盟所在地供应茶水。出席者包括哥萨克联盟主席D. V. Kochnev上校、战争伤残军人联盟主席V. V. Zimin将军、P. P. Oglobin将军及许多人。收到了居住在大连的远东全体哥萨克首领G. M. Semionoff发来的贺电。

飞行员抵沪

P. E. Homiakoff先生于3月31日抵达。Homiakoff先生负责青岛港的航空事务，他飞往上海是为了熟悉从美国西科斯基工厂运至此地的两架新飞机。大战期间，Homiakoff先生在俄国与西科斯基共事。

有趣的讲座

著名法学家、《旧灯换新盏》（New Lamps for Old）一书作者A. M. Kolenev先生在前军官俱乐部就“根据最新调查研究的义和团起义”发表了有趣的演讲。Kotenev先生最近完成了他的新书《中国士兵》（Soldier of China），该书将以中文及其他语言出版。他收集了从古代至今中国军事历史的丰富资料。

支队周年纪念

上周四，在法警俱乐部举行了纪念晚宴，庆祝俄国分队成立五周年。由警务总监L. Fabre指挥官主持，分队全体军官出席了晚宴，法国警察高层和法公董局的许多代表也参加了。Fabre先生在对俄国分队发表的精彩演讲中表示，自F. L. Gleboff将军在1931年事变期间组建该分队以来，官兵始终表现出高度的责任感和荣誉感。在他们五年的服役期间，没有发生一次误会，没有一份不利报告，也没有一次需要训诫的情况。演讲结束时，当Fabre先生宣读所有因英勇而获得金质和铜质奖章的俄国官兵名单时，全体起立；Fabre先生指出，其中一些人在履行职责时献出了生命。

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, MONDAY, MARCH 29, 1937

IN THE
RUSSIAN
COLONY

By "STROY"

While Shanghai is not yet thinking of summer-resorts, Russians are already making preparations for that season. Outside of the Russian colony it is hardly known that according to official reports of the Passport Bureau, there were last summer no less than 2,000 Russians holiday-making in Tsingtao alone. Russians were always fond of going to health-resorts (datchas). Every Russian city, whether large or small, is certain to have a place of rest somewhere on its outskirts. Resorts on the Caucasus, the Crimea, and others, grew with incredible speed; and even in emigration, Russians have retained this passion for leaving the city during the summer months.

In Harbin, for example, as soon as Russians arrived there in 1920, health-resorts in Manchuria: Chalantun, Ertzetziatze, Fuliaherdi, Barim, etc., began to grow, to use a Russian expression, "like mushrooms after a shower." Nearly every railway station was converted into a health-resort, and here Russian health-seekers and some foreigners as well began to arrive even from Shanghai.

Prior to the influx of Russians into Harbin, no one thought it possible that the muddy and treacherous river Sungari could be used for bathing. After 1920, on almost every sunny summer day thousands crossed to the opposite bank, where they not only swam, but for hours lay in the sun, sat in hundreds of little cafes and restaurants which had sprung up, had their tiffin and even their dinner, and only after sunset returned to the city—sunburnt, spent but satisfied.

In Shanghai, Russians are likewise making heroic attempts to "discover" places which can be converted into datchas. They first opened Chapoo as a summer-resort; there they began to buy up land, build small cottages, and make the beach usable. The declaration of Chapoo a military zone, however, made this dream impossible. Then their attention was turned to Pootoo, and to that holy island they organized weekly trips. But there is a limited supply of food in Pootoo; it is forbidden to eat meat there; and communication facilities are inconvenient. Last year Russians started to build summer houses on Point Island, and formed a Scout camp in Zose; but, unfortunately, a score of boys caught schistosomiasis. Thus, Tsingtao remains the nearest and most popular summer-resort, although many Russians leave for Peitaiho and the beaches of Dairen and Chefoo.

An Industry

The resort business is becoming in its own way an industry. With the coming of March, enterprising Russian men and women sell for Tsingtao and rent houses which they turn into boarding-houses. This year the Russian Orthodox Confraternity is opening a large rest house in Laoshan, where most of the houses belong to, or are exploited by, Russians. There is no branch of the summer-season trade in which Russians do not take a lively part. Musicians, painters, manicurists, chefs, chauffeurs, dentists, doctors—even tutors to pique backward pupils—all leave for Tsingtao.

To Russians a summer resort is more necessary than to members of other nationalities. They have no spacious houses with lawns, no cars in which to take rides in the country. The majority of them do not belong to clubs with swimming pools. They live in narrow, stuffy apartments, and to them a summer resort is, therefore, a question of health.

Business College

On March 25 the Russian Business College situated in Rue Cardinal Mercier (in the Girls' High School of the Russian Women's League) celebrated its first anniversary. The principal of this College is Mr. B. I. Eltekov. In addition to book-keeping, accountancy and banking, the curriculum includes mercantile law, political economy, and the lore of things Chinese. It is generally hoped that the Russian Business College will be the embryo of a future Russian University. In Shanghai there has already been formed an academic centre, the representative of which is Prof. M. P. Golovacheff, and in the autumn several professors from Harbin are expected. The idea of founding in Shanghai an independent university with Russian professors, or a Russian faculty in one of the existing local universities, has the warm support of Prof. G. G. Telberg, a famous Russian jurist residing since the revolution in Tsingtao.

Church to Be Enlarged

St. Andrew's Church in Route Valton, which is very popular among its members, is having its building enlarged. But in spite of the process of renovation, services, as in all other Russian Churches, are held daily on account of Great Lent. March 24 marked the 136th anniversary of the murder of Emperor Paul I; and on that day Bishop John conducted in St. Nicholas Military Church in Rue Corneille the requiem service for the deaths of Emperors Paul I, Alexander II, and Nicholas II—the three Emperors of All Russia who met death at the hands of their fellow men.

Last Saturday Russian artillerists—former boarders of the Constantine Military College held an anniversary dinner at the Ex-Officers' Club in Rue Lafayette, which was attended not only by the artillerists themselves, but by many other officers of the Imperial Army & Navy.

Medical Society Meets

Last week members of the Russian Medical Society held their annual meeting. Dr. D. I. Kasakov gave a lecture on the application of the new method of curing tuberculosis of the lungs; and demonstrated his talk with films and with patients. The President of the Society, Dr. A. V. Tarle, thanked the speaker who had laboured long over his papers and had given much new and interesting information.

Art Exhibition

In the near future there will be an exhibition of the drawings of A. A. Efimoff, the well-known artist, who specialises in the refined art of miniature portraits. The exhibition will be held in the premises of the International Arts Theatre. Mr. Efimoff is well known in Shanghai and Tsingtao, where he made many of his extraordinary miniature portraits in ivory.

D.S.I. Lohofiev
J.L '37

《字林西报》，1937年3月29日，星期一

在
俄国
侨民区

作者：“STROY”

虽然上海人尚未考虑避暑胜地之事，但俄国人已在为该季节做准备。在俄国侨民区之外，人们几乎不知道，根据护照局的官方报告，去年夏天仅在青岛度假的俄国人就不少于2,000人。俄国人一直喜爱前往疗养地（datchas）。无论大小，每座俄国城市肯定在其郊外某处设有休憩之地。高加索、克里米亚等地的避暑胜地以惊人的速度发展；即便在流亡生活中，俄国人仍保留着在夏季月份离开城市的这种嗜好。

例如在哈尔滨，俄国人于1920年抵达那里后，满洲里的疗养地：扎兰屯、二道河子、富拉尔基、巴林等，便如雨后春笋般涌现——用一句俄国谚语来说，“像阵雨后的蘑菇”。几乎每个火车站都变成了疗养地，来自上海甚至其他地方的俄国疗养者以及一些外国人开始汇聚于此。

在俄国人涌入哈尔滨之前，没人认为浑浊且危险的松花江可用于沐浴。1920年以后，在几乎每一个阳光明媚的夏日，成千上万的人渡江到对岸，他们不仅游泳，还长时间躺在阳光下，坐在如雨后春笋般出现的数百家小咖啡馆和餐馆里，吃午餐甚至晚餐，直到日落后才返回城市——皮肤晒黑，疲惫但满足。

在上海，俄国人同样做出英勇尝试，去“发现”那些可以改造成别墅（datchas）的地方。他们首先将闸北开辟为避暑胜地；在那里，他们开始购买土地，建造小屋，并使海滩变得可用。然而，宣布闸北为军事区使这一梦想成为泡影。随后，他们的注意力转向了普陀，并组织了前往那座神圣岛屿的每周旅行。但普陀的食物供应有限；那里禁止吃肉；且交通设施不便。去年，俄国人开始在Point Island（音译）建造避暑房屋，并在Zose（音译）建立了一个童子军营地；但不幸的是，约有二十名男孩感染了血吸虫病。因此，青岛仍然是最近且最受欢迎的避暑胜地，尽管许多俄国人前往北戴河以及大连和烟台的海滩。

一项产业

避暑生意正以其自身方式成为一种产业。随着三月的到来，富有进取心的俄国男女出售前往青岛的名额，并出租他们改造成寄宿公寓的房屋。今年，俄罗斯东正教兄弟会将在崂山开设一家大型休养所，那里的大部分房屋属于俄国人或由俄国人经营。在夏季季节性贸易的任何分支中，俄国人都积极参与。音乐家、画家、美甲师、厨师、司机、牙医、医生——甚至是辅导落后学生的家庭教师——全都前往青岛。

对俄国人而言，避暑胜地比其他国籍的人更为必要。他们没有带草坪的宽敞房屋，没有可驾车下乡的汽车。他们大多数人也不属于拥有游泳池的俱乐部会员。他们居住在狭窄、闷热的公寓里，因此，对他们来说，避暑胜地是一个关乎健康的问题。

商业学院

3月25日，位于麦尔西爱路（Rue Cardinal Mercier，在俄国妇女联盟女子中学内）的俄国商业学院庆祝了其成立一周年。该学院院长为B. I. Eltekov先生。除了簿记、会计和银行业务外，课程还包括商法、政治经济学和中国常识。人们普遍希望，俄国商业学院将成为未来俄国大学的雏形。在上海已经形成了一个学术中心，其代表人物是M. P. Golovacheff教授，预计秋季将有几位来自哈尔滨的教授加入。关于在上海创办一所拥有俄国教授的独立大学，或在现有本地大学之一中设立俄国院系的想法，得到了著名俄国法学家G. G. Telberg教授的热情支持，他自革命以来一直居住在青岛。

教堂将扩建

位于华尔顿路（Route Valton）的圣安德烈教堂深受其教徒欢迎，目前正在进行建筑扩建。尽管处于翻新过程中，但由于大斋期，礼拜活动如同所有其他俄国教堂一样每日举行。3月24日是保罗一世皇帝遇刺136周年纪念日；当天，约翰主教在科乃尔路（Rue Corneille）的圣尼古拉军人教堂主持了追思礼拜，悼念保罗一世、亚历山大二世和尼古拉二世这三位死于同胞之手的全俄罗斯皇帝。

上周六，俄国炮兵军官——前康斯坦丁军事学院的寄宿生——在拉斐德路（Rue Lafayette）的前军官俱乐部举行了周年纪念晚宴，出席者不仅有炮兵军官本人，还有许多前帝国陆海军的其他军官。

医学会召开会议

上周，俄国医学会成员举行了年度会议。D. I. Kasakov博士发表了关于应用治疗肺结核新方法的演讲；并通过电影和患者演示了他的讲话。学会主席A. V. Tarle博士感谢了这位长期致力于论文研究并提供了大量新颖有趣信息的演讲者。

艺术展览

近期将举办著名艺术家A. A. Efimoff的画作展览，他专攻精致的微型肖像画艺术。展览将在国际艺术剧院举行。Efimoff先生在上海和青岛颇有名气，他在那里创作了许多非凡的象牙微型肖像画。

D.S.I. Lohofiev
J.L '37

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, MONDAY, MARCH 22, 1937

IN THE
RUSSIAN
COLONY

By SMYOV

The Russian Chamber of Commerce answered the local branch of the Kuomintang in regard to registration in conformity with Chinese Law. The Russian Chamber of Commerce, the only association of its kind which unites all Russian businessmen in the city, has been in existence for five years. The slowness of registration, is explained by the fact that Chinese authorities recently discussed the whole question of Russians in China, and particularly in Shanghai. It was decided that in future the Government will allow Russian emigrants to govern themselves in their internal affairs, controlling their activities through representative organs such as the Emigration Committee, the United Russian Association (SORO) or the Russian Chamber of Commerce, all of which would be registered by the Chinese authorities.

In a statement to the press, Mr. A. G. Chibunovsky, vice-president of the Chamber of Commerce, said that Russian businessmen have decided to study thoroughly the industries of China in order to be able to act as channels through which the products of these industries could be directed to the public—principally, of course, the Russian Community.

Mr. Chibunovsky welcomed the appearance of banks in the Russian market—banks which have dealings largely with Russian businessmen; and mentioned that the new Discount Savings Bank has been built on old Russian banking principles. At present the Russian Chamber of Commerce gives this bank, as well as others, information on the credit value of individual Russian businessmen, and sometimes supports applications of its members for loans. Mr. Chibunovsky remarked that even at present foreign and Chinese banks find it difficult to work in accord with local Russian businessmen; "They do not yet understand," he says, "the Russian businessman: they do not understand the conditions in which he has to work or the methods which he has to employ."

This perhaps explains why the Russian colony at present has at its disposal—if the expression can be used —five banks which it considers its own: the Discount Savings Bank in the Bearn Apartments Building in Avenue Joffre, the Asiatic Credit Company in Rue Cardinal Mercier, the Russian Mutual Credit Corporation in Avenue Foch, the Russo-Chinese Credit Co-operative Society in Route Paul Henri, and opened last week opposite the Cercle Sportif Francais—the Banque de Crédit Commercial & Shanghai.

In addition, the Russian Chamber of Commerce itself registers Russian firms, and gives letters of recommendation to businessmen for presentation in foreign Embassies and Consulates, and for facilitating the obtaining of visas for travel abroad. The season has just arrived when many Russians go to Japan, to America, and to Europe, for mercantile affairs. Animation is being noticed in Russian commercial circles, and many are trying to stock up commodities, at the place of production, thus hoping that in autumn they may have the goods in Shanghai.

100,000th Patient

On Wednesday, March 17, the Ambulatory of the Russian Orthodox Confraternity registered its 100,-000th patient. This Ambulatory renders medical help principally to the indigent in the Community. It was opened on October 8, 1923, at 235 Avenue Foch, directly after the first wave of Russian refugees from Vladivostok reached Shanghai. The foundation of its activities was laid by the American Red Cross, which donated $1,350. This money was spent in paying for and renovating the building, and in purchasing furniture, requisite medical instruments and material necessary for dressing. The attention to 100,000 patients, however, has not been the whole work of the Ambulatory for Russian indigents. During all this time the Ambulatory has distributed free medicine on 120,000 doctors' prescriptions, has given hundreds of thousands of injections, thousands of operations, massages, etc. In addition to this the Ambulatory daily gives medical help of urgent character in cases of accident, poisoning, wounds, attempted suicides, etc.

Weddings Cease

With the coming of the Great Lent, weddings will not be held in Russian churches for seven weeks, right up to Russian Easter. Counting the number of marriages solemnized in Russian churches during the year, the Bishop's chancellory has found the total less than in the past. In order to be married with benefit of the Russian Orthodox Church it is necessary to make a statement to this effect to clerical authorities, and present several indispensable documents. Then the names of the couple, giving their places of birth and stating what nationalities they are, are published in the "Church Messenger" and the Russian newspapers. The week following Easter is called the "Red Hill" week; and this is the most popular season for Russian weddings. Everyone tries to celebrate their nuptial ceremonies on "Red Hill" week.

Publication Centre

Low cost of labour and modern methods of printing are responsible for making Shanghai a centre for the publishing of Russian books. Last year there were more books in the Russian language printed in Shanghai than in Paris, Berlin or even Riga. In the near future the printing of the famous journal "Sovremennye Zapiski" ("Annales Contemporaines") will be transferred from Paris to Shanghai. This paper—the only existing large monthly literary and political magazine printed in the Russian language —has been established ten years and prints the work of such famous contemporary Russian authors as Ivan Bunin, winner of the Nobel Prize, D. S. Merejkowski, A. M. Aldanov, A. I. Kuprin and others.

The National Committee of the Russian Merchant Association under the leadership of Commander N. G. Formin and Col. G. K. Biologov are, with the coming of spring, busy organising a large camp for children in Tientsin. Russian parents are invited to send their children to this country where the air is pure. The cost will be but 60 taels monthly, and the children will be efficiently under the supervision of experienced leaders.

（手写批注：J.C. 2/3）
（手写批注：S.1 / 28R. / 23/3）

《字林西报》，1937年3月22日，星期一

在
俄国
侨民区

作者：SMYOV

俄国商会就依照中国法律进行注册一事，答复了国民党当地分部。俄国商会是本市联合所有俄国商人的唯一此类协会，已成立五年。注册进展缓慢的原因在于，中国当局最近讨论了在华俄国人、特别是在上海俄国人的整个问题。会议决定，今后政府将允许俄国移民在其内部事务上实行自治，并通过诸如移民委员会、全俄联合会（SORO）或俄国商会等代表机构对其活动进行监管，这些机构均将由中国当局注册。

商会副会长 A. G. Chibunovsky 先生在对新闻界的声明中表示，俄国商人已决定深入研究中国的工业，以便能够作为渠道，将这些工业的产品导向公众——当然主要是俄国社区。

Chibunovsky 先生欢迎银行进入俄国市场——这些银行主要与俄国商人开展业务；并提到新的贴现储蓄银行是依据旧的俄国银行原则建立的。目前，俄国商会向该银行及其他银行提供有关个别俄国商人信用价值的信息，有时还支持其成员的贷款申请。Chibunovsky 先生指出，即使目前，外国和中国银行也觉得难以与当地俄国商人协调工作；他说：“他们尚不了解‘俄国商人’：他们不了解他必须工作的环境或必须采用的方法。”

这或许解释了为什么俄国侨民区目前拥有——如果可以使用这个表述的话——五家被视为其自有的银行：位于霞飞路（Avenue Joffre）Bearn 公寓大楼的贴现储蓄银行，位于梅神父路（Rue Cardinal Mercier）的亚洲信贷公司，位于福煦路（Avenue Foch）的俄国互助信贷公司，位于保罗亨利路（Route Paul Henri）的俄中信贷合作社，以及上周在法国总会（Cercle Sportif Francais）对面开业的上海商业信贷银行（Banque de Crédit Commercial & Shanghai）。

此外，俄国商会本身负责注册俄国商行，并向商人出具推荐信，以便向外国大使馆和领事馆出示，并协助获取出国旅行的签证。许多俄国人前往日本、美国和欧洲处理商务的季节刚刚到来。俄国商界注意到活跃气氛，许多人试图在生产地储备商品，希望能在秋季将货物运抵上海。

第10万名患者

3月17日星期三，俄国东正教兄弟会门诊部登记了其第100,000名患者。该门诊部主要为社区内的贫困者提供医疗帮助。它于1923年10月8日在福煦路235号开设，正值第一批来自海参崴的俄国难民抵达上海之后不久。其活动基础由美国红十字会奠定，后者捐赠了1,350美元。这笔钱用于支付和翻新建筑，以及购买家具、必要的医疗器械和包扎材料。然而，诊治10万名患者并非该俄国贫民门诊部的全部工作。在此期间，门诊部凭医生处方免费发放了12万份药物，进行了数十万次注射、数千次手术、按摩等。此外，门诊部每日还为事故、中毒、受伤、自杀未遂等紧急情况提供医疗救助。

婚礼暂停

随着大斋期的到来，俄国教堂将在七周内不举行婚礼，直至俄国复活节。主教公署统计了全年在俄国教堂举行的婚礼数量，发现总数少于往年。若要获得俄国东正教会的祝福而结婚，必须向神职当局提交相关声明，并提交几份必备文件。随后，夫妇双方的姓名、出生地及国籍将在《教会信使》和俄国报纸上刊登。复活节后的一周被称为“红山”周；这是俄国婚礼最受欢迎的季节。每个人都试图在“红山”周举行婚礼仪式。

出版中心

低廉的劳动力成本和现代的印刷方法使上海成为俄国书籍的出版中心。去年在上海印刷的俄文书籍比在巴黎、柏林甚至里加印刷的还要多。在不久的将来，著名期刊《现代纪事》（"Sovremennye Zapiski" / "Annales Contemporaines"）的印刷工作将从巴黎转移至上海。这份刊物是唯一现存的大型俄文月刊文学和政治杂志，已创办十年，刊登了诸如诺贝尔奖得主伊万·布宁（Ivan Bunin）、D. S. Merejkowski、A. M. Aldanov、A. I. Kuprin 等著名当代俄国作家的作品。

在指挥官 N. G. Formin 和 G. K. Biologov 上校的领导下，俄国商人协会全国委员会正趁着春季来临，忙于在天津组织一个大型儿童营地。邀请俄国父母将孩子送到这个空气清新的地方。费用仅为每月60两白银，孩子们将在经验丰富的领导者的有效监督之下。

The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Thursday, March 4, 1937
19744

White Russian
Immigrants Hit
By Chinese Ban

Restriction On Influx
Into China Planned
By Nanking

SOCIETIES PUT
ON NEW BASIS

Activities Of Russians
In South Said Cause
Of Action

By PHILIP KING
White Russians in China, who constitute the largest single European group in the Far East, are to have their movements restricted henceforth. Drastic restrictions on immigration into China Proper and closer control of Russians living here are imminent, the Shanghai Evening Post learned today.

It is believed that reports from Canton concerning the large number of White Russians allegedly engaged in "doubtful activities" or "a certain country" in the South have had the effect of bringing about action on the part of Nanking in regard to Russian status in China.

Sora Reorganized

First step in instrumenting this policy of closer scrutiny over Russian affairs has been the recent reorganization of the United Russian Public Organizations, known as the Sora, by order of the Chinese government. The Sora will henceforth be recognized as an official representative organization of all Russians living in China, according to Mr. P. T. Tsao, a director of the People's Training and Movement Department of the local Kuomintang Headquarters.

In an exclusive interview with the Post today, Mr. Tsao revealed that the Sora was closed down eight months ago by Nanking, a fact unknown to the majority of the 25,000 Russians resident in Shanghai.

No Representation

For three months, from last July to October, Russians in China theoretically had no official representative organization, as the Russian Immigrants Committee was not registered in Nanking until November. Most Russians were unaware of this state of affairs and despite government closure the organization continued to function throughout the period, Mr. Tsao stated.

The Sora and the Immigrants Committee, rival organizations which have never enjoyed the best of relations, have both been reorganized through a decision reached by the Chinese authorities, and thereafter the government will deal with Russian problems through these organizations.

Increase In Fees

Major changes in regulations covering visas and passports for Russian immigrants will be announced in the near future, it is understood, though an official notice has not yet been issued. A sharp increase in the fees for visas is expected, in order to check the influx of Russians from "Manchukuo", many of whom are now considered undesirable elements by the Chinese authorities. Restrictions on immigration are expected to be clamped down soon.

An effective way to instrument this is to increase rates. Russians now living in China pay $3 for a certificate of registration with the government, and $4 for a passport to entitle them to travel inside China Proper. A visa allowing a Russian to leave the country and return after a short period was formerly $1, but last December the fee was increased to $4.

Now Must Pay

Russians who formerly desired to enter China from abroad as immigrants could come into the country without paying anything. Now, however, Russian immigrants are paying a stipulated sum, it is learned.

Individual cases cited include that of a Russian who went to the United States recently for a short visit and had to pay U.S.$20 for a visa at the Chinese Consulate-General in Los Angeles in order to return. A Russian officer attached to the Shanghai Municipal Police paid $610 for a return visa when he left for Europe on a holiday a short time ago. Another Russian leaving England for China paid £5 for his visa.

Groups Quarreled

The Sora, headed by General F. I. Gleboff, and the Immigrants Committee, headed by Mr. Charles E. Matafer, formerly vice-consul in Shanghai for the Czarist Government, have not been on the best of terms, and the Russian community in Shanghai is aware that there has been continued differences of opinion between these two organizations.

Because of this, according to Mr. Tsao, Nanking decided not to deal with the Sora, but immediately petitions poured in from both organizations. Seeing the futility of recognizing only one organization, Nanking authorities decided that the best course under the circumstances was to deal through both beginning March 1.

Major Problem

It is understood that these new measures and those that are expected to go into effect shortly will apply as well to other foreign nationals who do not enjoy extraterritorial rights, but it is generally presumed that the plans were formulated largely for Russian affairs in particular.

The problem of the welfare of Russian immigrants in China is one of the major questions, as the Russians constitute the largest European group in the country.

《上海晚邮报与水星报》，1937年3月4日，星期四
19744

白俄
移民遭
中国禁令打击

南京计划
限制进入
中国境内

社团改组
为新基础

据称俄国人在
南方的活动
是采取行动的原因

作者：菲利普·金（Philip King）
在华白俄构成了远东地区最大的单一欧洲人群体，其行动今后将受到限制。《上海晚邮报》今日获悉，对进入中国内地的移民实施严厉限制，以及对在此居住的俄国人进行更严密的管控，已迫在眉睫。

据信，来自广州的有关大量白俄 allegedly 在南方从事“可疑活动”或为“某国”效力的报告，促使南京方面就俄国人在华地位问题采取了行动。

索拉重组

实施这项加强对俄事务审查政策的第一步，是中国政府下令近期重组了联合俄国公共组织（United Russian Public Organizations），即众所周知的“索拉”（Sora）。据当地国民党总部民众训练与运动部主任曹先生（P. T. Tsao，音译）称，索拉今后将被承认为所有在华俄籍居民的官方代表组织。

曹先生今日在接受本报独家采访时透露，索拉于八个月前被南京当局关闭，这一事实不为居住在上海的25,000名俄国人中的大多数人所知。

无代表机构

从去年七月到十月这三个月期间，在华俄国人理论上没有官方代表组织，因为俄侨委员会直到十一月才在南京注册。曹先生表示，大多数俄国人并不知晓这一状况，尽管政府已下令关闭，该组织在此期间仍继续运作。

索拉与俄侨委员会这两个从未保持良好关系的 rival 组织，均通过中国当局的决定进行了重组，此后政府将通过这些组织处理俄国人的问题。

费用增加

据悉，涵盖俄籍移民签证和护照的法规将在近期宣布重大变更，尽管官方通知尚未发布。预计签证费用将大幅上涨，以遏制来自“满洲国”的俄国人涌入，其中许多人目前被中国当局视为不良分子。预计移民限制将很快严格执行。

实施这一措施的有效方法是提高费率。目前居住在中国的俄国人向政府支付3美元办理登记证，支付4美元办理护照以便在中国内地旅行。允许俄国人出境并在短期后回国的签证以前收费1美元，但去年十二月费用已增至4美元。

现在必须付费

据悉，以前希望从国外作为移民进入中国的俄国人可以无需支付任何费用入境。然而现在，俄籍移民需支付规定金额。

 cited 的个人案例包括：一名俄国人最近前往美国短期访问，为了返回中国，不得不在洛杉矶的中国总领事馆支付20美元办理签证。一名隶属于上海公共租界工部局警务处的俄国军官不久前休假前往欧洲时，支付了610美元办理回程签证。另一名从英国前往中国的俄国人支付了5英镑办理签证。

团体争吵

由格列博夫将军（General F. I. Gleboff）领导的索拉，与由前沙皇政府驻上海副领事查尔斯·E·马塔弗尔先生（Mr. Charles E. Matafer）领导的俄侨委员会，关系一直不佳，上海俄裔社区深知这两个组织之间持续存在意见分歧。

据曹先生称，正因为如此，南京决定不与索拉打交道，但随即两个组织都递交了请愿书。南京当局看到仅承认一个组织的徒劳，决定在这种情况下最好的做法是从3月1日起同时与两个组织打交道。

主要问题

据悉，这些新措施以及预计即将生效的措施也将适用于其他不享有治外法权的外国国民，但人们普遍推测，这些计划主要是针对俄国人事务而制定的。

在华俄籍移民的福利问题是主要问题之一，因为俄国人构成了该国最大的欧洲人群体。

213
（批注：档案 5/3 437）

THE SHANGHAI SUNDAY TIMES, JULY 12, 1936
508314

Origin And Future Of The
Local Russian Community

First Of Series Of Interesting Articles Having
Historical And Sociological Value; How 22,000
Strangers Came To Be Domiciled Here

Recent developments in Manchoukuo have reacted unfavourably on the condition of Russian residents in that country. Many, particularly those living at Harbin, have been compelled to leave. The result has been a new exodus southwards, and in the last twelve months the Shanghai Russian Community has grown considerably and is still growing.

At the same time the dispute within its ranks as to which of two bodies—S.O.R.O. and the Russian Emigrants Committee—is to be regarded as its official agent vis-a-vis the Chinese authorities has again become acute.

The following is the first of a series of articles on Shanghai's Russian Community, its origin, history, organization and future prospects, which has been specially written for "The Shanghai Sunday Times" by a well-known student of local affairs. The series, which should prove of timely interest to readers, will be continued each Sunday for five weeks.

On the outbreak of the Great War, in 1914, Imperial Russia had in China considerable trading interests, the headquarters of which were mostly in Shanghai, and to look after these interests and the interests of her nationals generally she maintained a Consul-General and staff in the building now occupied by the representatives of the Soviet Government. The Russian community though small in numbers—it was little over a hundred strong—was a wealthy, cultured and influential one, often having a representative on the Municipal Council of the International Settlement.

The first considerable increase in the size of this community occurred after Germany's occupation of Poland in 1916/7, when many refugees arrived from that area. Then came the Revolution, and with the steady roll of the Red tide eastwards and particularly after the fall of Admiral Kolchak's government at Omsk in 1919, the Russian community steadily grew. By 1922 the number of refugees in Shanghai was estimated to lie between two and three thousand, and their presence had already begun to present a difficult problem. They had to be kept decently alive, and, if possible, found employment, and in 1919 a Refugee Relief Committee was formed to aid them. The following year, in July 1920, the refugees themselves formed a Russian Military Union which did a great deal to help the more distressed of their fellows. By the end of 1921 the position had grown acute enough to call for leading articles in the local press, particularly in relation to the straits to which the women were reduced in order to maintain themselves.

At the same time anxiety was being aroused in the minds not only of other foreigners but of the Russians themselves by the character and behaviour of some of these earlier arrivals, many of them ex-members of those bands of White Guards whose methods of waging war in Siberia had come in for not a little criticism. The deportation of undesirables was suggested, and also that new comers should not be admitted without passports, but the peculiar conditions of Shanghai, the chaotic state of China and the difficulties of discovering any deporting authority or any destination to which the deportees might be sent made such proposals hard to carry out.

It is only fair to emphasize here that it was very largely a case of a few black sheep giving the whole body a bad name. These early letters to the papers form almost the only examples of the conduct of the Russian refugees coming in for unfavourable criticism.

Vladivostock Falls

In view of what was to happen in the next 18 months, these anxieties and alarms of 1921 seem rather disproportionate to the occasion. In October, 1922, the last White Russian stronghold, Vladivostock, which had been holding out with Japanese support collapsed as Japan withdrew the last of her troops and liquidated a Siberian adventure which had proved more or less a dead loss. Thus left to their fate, the only recourse left to the White Russians, whether soldiers or civilians was flight. Persecution and possible death was only too certainly their lot if they remained to submit to the triumphant Red armies. Some made their way on foot into Manchuria, but the majority, hastily collecting such scanty belongings as they could carry, piled themselves, men, women and children, on board any ships they could commandeer, and put out to sea.

The first stop was Gensan in Korea, 300 odd miles to the south. Early in November 26 ships, under Admiral Stark, arrived there, and soon some 9,000 refugees were herded together in such scanty accommodation as could be improvised. Those provided with money and passports gradually went off to Manchuria, but these formed only a small minority.

Two Thousand At Woosung

At the end of November, Admiral Stark set out again, this time with 14 ships carrying over 2,000 unfortunates, including the 350 orphaned sons of Russian soldiers, the pupils of two cadet schools, one from Khabarovsk, the other from Omsk. This rather bedraggled flotilla—the ships were small, poorly furnished, not too seaworthy and very overcrowded—fetched up off Woosung on December 9 much to the embarrassment of the local authorities, both foreign and Chinese. Many of the men were soldiers, still armed and in uniform, and there was ammunition on board.

Shanghai was the nearest port, and the refugees applied for permission to land. Pending that, convenient guests. Pending that, permission to land was refused them. However, the flotilla was in no condition to move on; it had not coal enough for one thing, nor food either. Moreover the plight of the schoolboys and of the women and other children was too bad to be ignored. Only the grossest inhumanity could have failed to respond to their obvious and urgent need, and eventually the schools and some hundreds of other civilians were allowed ashore. Coal and provisions were then given to Admiral Stark, and he sailed off to the Philippines, which he reached with the loss of two ships which foundered on the way. Six hundred of the men with him were fortunate enough to be taken almost immediately to the United States on board an army transport. The two hundred who remained behind, living mainly, off the proceeds of the sale of the ships, slowly dispersed, many of them back to Shanghai, and when he had seen the last man accounted for Admiral Stark himself went to Paris to earn his living as a common carrier driving his own motor-lorry.

General Gleboff Arrives

Over a thousand were thus added almost overnight to Shanghai's Russian population and responsibilities. Before 1923 was out nearly 2,000 more were to arrive, the majority from Gensan. On September 14, 1923, three small ships, all under 2,000 tons with a tender of 250 tons in attendance, dropped anchor off Woosung. On board were 852 men, no women and children. The fears of the previous December renewed themselves in the minds of the authorities, and with considerable reason. This was definitely a military force, armed with rifles, machine guns, mills bombs and hand grenades, and supplied with two million rounds of ammunition. Naturally the Chinese wished them away; unfortunately General Gleboff had no particular desire to move on—where was he to move to? In any case, his ships needed extensive repairs, and to be repaired they would have to move up the river and no-one wanted them and their formidable occupants so near Shanghai. They were told to stay at Woosung. Nor could the personnel be allowed to land without first surrendering their arms. A regiment 850 strong at the hire of the highest bidder was too dangerous a factor to let loose into the military and political rivalries of the time. Naturally, the Russians refused to surrender what was practically their only asset, though they were willing to sell if they could find a buyer. But though many a Chinese general would have liked to buy, no one dared do so for fear of precipitating a quarrel with the rest. So matters were at a deadlock and remained so.

在沪俄国侨民群体的起源与未来

系列有趣文章之首篇，具有历史与社会学价值；两万两千名异乡人如何在此定居

满洲国近期的事态发展对该国俄国居民的处境产生了不利影响。许多人，尤其是居住在哈尔滨者，被迫离开。其结果是出现了新一轮向南的逃亡潮，而在过去十二个月中，上海俄国侨民群体显著扩大，且仍在增长之中。

与此同时，该群体内部关于两个机构——S.O.R.O.（俄国侨民组织）与俄国难民委员会——哪一个应被视为面对中国当局时的官方代表机构的争论，再次变得尖锐起来。

以下是一系列关于上海俄国侨民群体及其起源、历史、组织和未来前景的文章中的第一篇，由一位熟知本地事务的知名人士专为《上海星期日报》撰写。该系列文章预计将引起读者的适时关注，并将连续五个星期日刊登。

1914年大战爆发时，沙皇俄国在中国拥有庞大的贸易利益，其总部大多设在上海。为了维护这些利益以及其国民的整体利益，俄国在如今由苏联政府代表所占据的大楼内设有总领事馆及工作人员。当时的俄国侨民群体虽然人数不多——仅一百余人——但却是一个富有、有文化且有影响力的群体，甚至经常在国际租界工部局董事会中拥有代表。

该群体规模的第一次显著增长发生在1916/17年德国占领波兰之后，当时许多难民从该地区涌入。随后爆发了革命，随着红色浪潮稳步向东推进，特别是在1919年高尔察克海军上将在鄂木斯克的政府垮台之后，俄国侨民群体稳步壮大。到1922年，估计上海的难民人数在两千至三千人之间，他们的存在已经开始成为一个棘手的问题。必须维持他们体面的生存，并尽可能为他们提供就业机会，因此在1919年成立了一个难民救济委员会来援助他们。次年，即1920年7月，难民们自己组建了一个俄国军人联盟，为帮助那些处境更为艰难的同胞做了大量工作。到1921年底，局势已变得十分严峻，以至于当地报刊，特别是针对妇女为维持生计而陷入的困境，发表了社论予以关注。

与此同时，不仅其他外国人，就连俄国人自己也因这些早期抵达者的品行和行为而感到焦虑，其中许多人是前白卫军成员，他们在西伯利亚的作战方式曾受到不少批评。有人建议驱逐不受欢迎的人，并规定新来者若无护照不得入境，但鉴于上海的特殊情况、中国的混乱状态，以及难以找到任何驱逐执行机构或可将被驱逐者送往的任何目的地，使得这些提议难以实施。

在此必须公平地强调，这很大程度上是个别害群之马使整个群体蒙受恶名的情况。这些早期投书报端的信件，几乎是俄国难民行为遭受不利批评的唯一例证。

符拉迪沃斯托克陷落

鉴于随后18个月内发生的事件，1921年的这些焦虑和警报似乎有些反应过度。1922年10月，最后一个白俄据点符拉迪沃斯托克（海参崴），在日本撤回最后部队并清算了一场或多或少血本无归的西伯利亚冒险行动后，随着日本支持的撤去而崩溃。被听任自生自灭的白俄人，无论是军人还是平民，唯一的出路就是逃亡。如果留下来向胜利的红军投降，等待他们的几乎肯定是迫害乃至死亡。一些人步行进入满洲，但大多数人匆忙收集能携带的少量财物，男女老少挤上任何能征用的船只，驶向大海。

第一站是向南约300英里的朝鲜元山。11月初，斯塔克海军上将率领的26艘船只抵达那里，不久约9,000名难民被聚集在临时凑合的简陋住所中。那些有钱和有护照的人逐渐前往满洲，但这只占少数。

吴淞的两千人

11月底，斯塔克海军上将再次出发，这次率领14艘船只，载有2,000多名不幸者，其中包括350名俄国士兵的孤儿，他们是两所士官学校的学生，一所来自哈巴罗夫斯克，另一所来自鄂木斯克。这支略显狼狈的小舰队——船只小巧，设施简陋，适航性不佳且极度拥挤——于12月9日停泊在吴淞口外，令当地中外当局都感到尴尬。许多人是士兵，仍全副武装并身着军装，船上还有弹药。

上海是最近的港口，难民申请登陆许可。在此期间，他们成了不便的客人。在此之前，他们的登陆请求被拒绝。然而，这支舰队已无法继续航行；一方面没有足够的煤炭，也没有食物。此外，军校学生、妇女和其他儿童的处境太糟糕，不容忽视。只有最无人性的做法才会对他们的明显且迫切的需求无动于衷，最终，学校人员和其他数百名平民获准上岸。随后向斯塔克海军上将提供了煤炭和补给，他启航前往菲律宾，途中因两艘船沉没而遭受损失。随行的六百名军人幸运地几乎立即被一艘陆军运输船带往美国。留下的两百人主要靠出售船只的收入为生，逐渐离散，其中许多人回到上海，而当斯塔克确认最后一名部下有着落后，他自己也前往巴黎，以驾驶自己的卡车从事普通运输业谋生。

格列博夫将军抵达

因此，上海的俄国人口和责任几乎在一夜之间增加了一千多人。在1923年结束之前，又有近2,000人抵达，大多数来自元山。1923年9月14日，三艘小型船只（均不足2,000吨）在一艘250吨的辅助船伴随下，在吴淞口外抛锚。船上有852名男子，没有妇女和儿童。去年12月的担忧在当局心中重现，且理由充分。这确实是一支军事力量，装备有步枪、机枪、米尔斯炸弹和手榴弹，并供应有两百万发子弹。中国人自然希望他们离开；不幸的是，格列博夫将军并没有特别的意愿继续前行——他能去哪里呢？无论如何，他的船只需要大规模修理，而要修理就必须驶入内河，但没有人希望他们及其令人畏惧的乘员如此靠近上海。他们被告知留在吴淞。此外，除非先缴械，否则不允许人员上岸。一支850人的团，待价而沽，若放入当时的军事和政治 rivalries（竞争/倾轧）中，是一个过于危险的因素。自然，俄国人拒绝交出实际上是他们唯一资产的东西，尽管如果有买主他们愿意出售。但是，虽然许多中国将军很想购买，但没人敢这么做，生怕引发与其他人的争执。因此，事情陷入僵局，并一直如此。

Origin Of Russian Regiment
For 12 months the flotilla remained at Woosung, and then. with a growing roll of sick and the condition of his men grow- ing steadily worse, the comman- der decided to take the law into his own hands. In September, 1924, he moved his ships into the Whangpoo to a position alongside the Quarantine Station and moor- ed there, at the same time com- mandeering an adjacent go-down as a hospital. Here the detach- ment remained, living on the sale of their arms and what monies General Gleboff could raise, until January 1927, when the S.M.C. allowed the 200 odd survivors to land. With rival Chinese forces at the Settlement gates it was glad to increase its defence forces enrolling 112 of the fittest into a paid detachment attached to the Volunteer Corps, a measure. it may be interesting to note, which had been mooted in the press as far back as August 1921. Thus originated the Russian Regiment. For the ships, General Gleboff managed to find purchasers.

Mutiny Breaks Out
The great decrease in the num- bers of the force was due to the heavy toll taken by death and sickness, a steady shrinkage as men managed to slip ashore into employment, and a mutiny. On March 11, 1925. at five minutes past seven in the morning; the tugboat Alexandria, belonging to the Shanghai Tug and Lighter Company, came alongside one of the ships, the s.s. Mongovgai, put a General Anisomoff on board along with some civilians, and then, going about, anchored about 100 yards off near a Chinese junk which had been detailed to watch the refugee squadron. A little later the men on the Mon- govgaï commenced to sever the hawsers connecting that ship to the s.s. Ochotsk, and on being challenged, returned no answer. Colonel Ivanow, commanding the Ochotsk, called his own men to arms only to be fired at from the Mongovgai, which fire he re- turned with his revolver. By this time the hawsers had been sever- ed, and the Ochotsk swung on to the shore. Colonel Ivanow then opened fire with 15 men and ordered two boats away to try to prevent the Mongovgai being removed, at the same time send- ing a third to the gunboat to ask for help. This was refused, the gun boat instead training her guns on the Ochotsk. Meanwhile, the Mongovgai had opened fire on the other two boats, and Ivanow ordered them back to the ship. A Chinese officer now went on board the tug, which proceeded to take the Mongovgai in tow. Colonel Ivanow kept up fire on the Mon- govgaï, taking care not to hit the tug, but to no purpose. The Mongovgai moved steadily away, and by nine o'clock was two miles distant up stream. Eventually with the 180 men on board her she returned to Vladivostock.

One other occurrence in connec- tion with this group is perhaps worth recording. By the terms of the Sino-Soviet Treaty of 1924, the Russian Consulate was to be handed over to Soviet representa- tives. General Gleboff, however, regarding the consulate as the pro- perty of the defunct Imperial Gov- ernment and as such not to be handed over without at least an emphatic protest from those who still remembered their allegiance to the Romanoffs, sent an armed detachment to occupy the building. Only the tactful persuasion of Captain Barrett of the S.M.P. pre- vented what might have been a nasty incident.

A Third Detachment
For a time another refugee ship was anchored alongside General Gleboff's boats at Woosung. On board were 700 ex-soldiers many of them skilled workmen known as the Ural-Siberian Group. At Gensan they had been employed in road and dike making by the Jap- anese, but the work was not per- manent, and when in June 1923, the representative of an American firm proposed that they should move south with their ship, the s.s. El Dorado, to Chekiang where he guaranteed them employment by the local Chinese authorities, they readily signed the agreement the day before them. When they reach- ed Chekiang, however, no work proved to be forthcoming and the agreement proved worthless. Until the autumn they stayed cooped up on Ninpo's on board ship with very little food and often short of water, and then moved up to Shanghai. Here they were re- duced to selling their arms, in which a brisk trade went on, a mat- ter of considerable local apprehen- sion. Gradually the 700 managed to make their way ashore, and eventually the ship was sold. Early in 1924 126 of these returned to the north, where Colonel Lebedeff had obtained work for them near Harbin on a C.E.R. railway con- struction.

On Foot From Sinkiang
Other refugees, of course, were arriving all the time, and the re- cord party body which arrived in this area in 1920 puts into the shade the stories even of the Gen- san groups. In their flight from the Bolsheviks many Russians had escaped into Sinkiang. There for years they endured great privation, and then, at the beginning of 1923, the Chinese authorities gave 800 of them 15 Chinese dollars apiece and put them across the border of the province to make what shift they could. A large number of two was hired to carry women and children, and the rest, old and ill-provided, started out on foot.

Growing steadily weaker for lack of food they trudged along; only the help of missionaries and an occasional friendly Chinese official saved them, and at last worn out, but without a single casualty, they reached Shanghai.

So the number of Russians grew and went on growing. The gen- eral strike of 1925 allowed many of them to find at least temporary employment, especially with the shipping companies. Here their work proved very satisfactory, so much so that Messrs. Butterfield and Swire, to mark their apprecia- tion, donated $5,000 to be used in relief work. Unfortunately the reports of this opening for employ- ment led to a new influx from the north where conditions were worse even than in Shanghai. By 1927 the Russian refugee population of Shanghai was over 8,000. Since then that figure has been nearly trebled, mainly by arrivals from Manchukuo, where first the Sino- Soviet troubles and then Japan's activities have materially affected for the worse the lot of the many thousands who settled there. They have had to pack up their belongings and move on again, and usually the place to which they have moved is Shanghai. It is in- deed almost the only place open to them.

To-day the Russian community here numbers over 22,000 and more are expected. Indeed some observ- ers believe that before another 12 months are out the figure will be 30,000.

(To be continued)

俄国团之起源

这支小舰队在吴淞停泊了十二个月，随后，由于病患名单日益增加，部下的状况持续恶化，指挥官决定自行其是。1924年9月，他将船只驶入黄浦江，停靠在检疫站旁并在此系泊，同时征用邻近的一座仓库作为医院。分队在此驻留，靠变卖武器以及格列博夫将军（General Gleboff）所能筹集的资金维持生计，直到1927年1月，上海公共租界工部局（S.M.C.）允许两百余名幸存者登陆。当时中国敌对势力兵临租界门口，工部局乐于增强防御力量，遂将其中身体最健壮的112人编入附属于万国商团的带薪分队。值得一提的是，此举早在1921年8月便已在报端被提出讨论。俄国团由此诞生。至于那些船只，格列博夫将军设法找到了买主。

爆发兵变

部队人数大幅减少，原因是死亡和疾病造成的惨重损失、人员不断偷偷上岸谋职导致的持续减员，以及一次兵变。1925年3月11日早上七点零五分，属于上海拖驳公司（Shanghai Tug and Lighter Company）的拖轮“亚历山大号”（Alexandria）靠上了一艘名为“蒙古盖号”（s.s. Mongovgai）的轮船，将阿尼索莫夫将军（General Anisomoff）及一些平民送上船，随后调头，在距一艘负责监视难民舰队的中国帆船约100码处抛锚。不久，“蒙古盖号”上的人员开始砍断将该船与“鄂霍次克号”（s.s. Ochotsk）相连的缆绳，面对质问，他们不予回应。指挥“鄂霍次克号”的伊万诺夫上校（Colonel Ivanow）召集手下武装戒备，却遭到“蒙古盖号”的射击，他用手枪予以还击。此时缆绳已被砍断，“鄂霍次克号”漂向岸边。伊万诺夫上校随即率领15人开火，并派出两艘小船试图阻止“蒙古盖号”被拖走，同时派遣第三艘小船前往炮艇求援。但求援被拒，炮艇反而将炮口对准了“鄂霍次克号”。与此同时，“蒙古盖号”向另外两艘小船开火，伊万诺夫命令它们返回大船。一名中国军官此时登上拖轮，拖轮随即开始拖带“蒙古盖号”。伊万诺夫上校持续向“蒙古盖号”射击，小心避免击中拖轮，但无济于事。“蒙古盖号”稳步驶离，到九点钟时已溯流而上至两英里外。最终，该船载着 aboard 的180人返回符拉迪沃斯托克（Vladivostock）。

与该群体有关的另一件事或许也值得记录。根据1924年《中苏条约》的规定，俄国领事馆应移交给苏联代表。然而，格列博夫将军视该领事馆为已覆灭的帝俄政府之财产，认为除非那些仍铭记对罗曼诺夫王朝效忠的人提出强烈抗议，否则不应移交，于是派遣武装分队占领了该建筑。唯有上海公共租界警务处（S.M.P.）巴雷特上尉（Captain Barrett）的巧妙劝解，才防止了一起可能发生的恶性事件。

第三支分队

有一段时间，另一艘难民船停泊在吴淞格列博夫将军的船只旁。船上有700名前士兵，其中许多人是熟练技工，被称为“乌拉尔-西伯利亚群体”（Ural-Siberian Group）。他们在元山（Gensan）受雇于日本人，从事修路和筑堤工作，但这份工作并非长期性质。1923年6月，一家美国公司的代表提议他们随其船只“埃尔多拉多号”（s.s. El Dorado）南下浙江，并保证当地中国当局会为他们提供工作，他们便于次日 readily 签署了协议。然而，当他们抵达浙江时，却发现并无工作机会，协议成了一纸空文。直到秋天，他们一直被困在宁波（Ninpo）的船上，食物极少，且经常缺水，随后他们北上前往上海。在这里，他们不得不变卖武器，武器交易颇为活跃，这引起了当地相当大的担忧。这700人逐渐设法上岸，最终船只也被出售。1924年初，其中126人返回北方，列别杰夫上校（Colonel Lebedeff）已在哈尔滨附近的中东铁路（C.E.R.）建设工地上为他们找到了工作。

从新疆徒步而来

当然，其他难民也在源源不断地到来，1920年抵达该地区的这一批难民，其经历甚至让元山群体的故事都相形见绌。在逃离布尔什维克的过程中，许多俄罗斯人逃入了新疆。在那里，他们多年来忍受着巨大的困苦，直到1923年初，中国当局发给其中800人每人15元中国货币，并将他们送出省界，让他们自谋生路。他们雇佣了大量脚夫来运送妇女和儿童，其余老弱病残、物资匮乏者则徒步出发。

由于缺乏食物，他们的体力日益衰弱，艰难跋涉；仅靠传教士的帮助和偶尔遇到的友善中国官员的援助才得以存活，最终，他们虽疲惫不堪，但未出现一人伤亡，抵达了上海。

因此，俄罗斯人的数量不断增长。1925年的大罢工使他们中的许多人至少找到了临时工作，尤其是在航运公司。他们的工作表现令人非常满意，以至于太古洋行（Butterfield and Swire）为表感激，捐赠了5,000美元用于救济工作。不幸的是，关于这一就业机会的消息导致了来自北方的新一波涌入，那里的情况甚至比上海更糟。到1927年，上海的俄罗斯难民人口已超过8,000人。此后，这一数字几乎增加了两倍，主要来自满洲国（Manchukuo）的抵达者，那里先是中苏纠纷，随后是日本的活动，严重恶化了定居在那里的数千人的处境。他们不得不收拾行囊再次迁徙，而通常他们的目的地就是上海。这确实几乎是他们唯一可去的地方。

如今，这里的俄罗斯社区人数超过22,000人，且预计还会有更多人来。事实上，一些观察家认为，在不到12个月内，这一数字将达到30,000人。

（待续）

page_data.en:
THE SHANGHAI SUNDAY TIMES

Origin And Future Of The
Local Russian Community

Second Of Series Of Interesting Articles Having
Local Historical Value; How The Problem Of
Refugees Taxed Resources Of Shanghai

Below will be found the second instalment of a series of five articles which have been specially written for "The Shanghai Sunday Times" dealing with Shanghai's Russian Community—its origin, history, organization and future prospects.

This instalment deals particularly with the problem which was created in 1923 by the presence of thousands of destitute Russian refugees in Shanghai, and tells of the organization of the Russians into a Russian Community and of the work that was done to improve their lot.

It would have been a difficult enough matter for any city to deal with such a large and sudden increase in its adult population as the arrival of the Russian refugees meant to Shanghai. For Shanghai it was especially difficult.

In the first place, the refugees were the responsibility, not of the city's total three million, but of a section of its 40,000 odd foreigners. In the second place, many avenues of employment were closed to the newcomers. In a European city they could, if all else failed, have joined the ranks of manual industrial and unskilled labour. Even if such work was not too well paid and implied a descent in the economic ladder, it would have entailed no loss of racial prestige or national self respect. In Shanghai such work is done by coolies at a wage far below that to which the humblest of the refugees was accustomed. Only by merging themselves in the Chinese coolie class and living among and as them could the refugees hope to maintain an existence in this way, and that, even if the language bar could have been overcome, was not a solution that recommended itself to anyone.

League Does Nothing

It was indeed a very difficult problem that confronted Shanghai and the Russians in the years immediately following 1922—one which both parties could reasonably expect the League of Nations to help them in solving. That body had set up a commission, headed by Dr. Nansen, especially to deal with war refugees, and England alone had donated £150,-000 for this work. In 1923 a report was made to the League on conditions in the Far East, and, in December, Dr. Grieg, of the Irish Presbyterian Mission at Kirin, was appointed delegate for China to the Nansen Commission. He was to make a thorough survey of the situation in order to find a "final solution for the Russian Refugee Problem in China."

His final recommendations were repatriation and emigration which did not help a great deal. The refugees could hardly be expected to return to the fate which awaited them at the hands of their red enemies, while emigration was out of the question without money to pay for their transportation and to secure their admittance into the country of their choice. As the refugees themselves were practically penniless and the League either would not or would not provide the necessary funds itself, the final solution was to leave the Russians to work out their own salvation with such help as foreign Shanghai could give them.

4,000 Destitute Russians

Of the need for help a report sent to the League from Shanghai in 1923 is eloquent testimony. More than half of the 7,000 odd Russians then in Shanghai were stated to be completely destitute, while the remainder earned a precarious living as clerks, shop assistants, chauffeurs, house servants, newspaper vendors and in doing odd jobs. They were living in insanitary houses in the poorest districts or even in single rooms in Chinese houses. They had no baths or mosquito nets, little furniture or bedding. The single daily meal of bread and soup at a soup kitchen was the only food many of them got, while most were inefficiently clad. There were no schools for the children, the babies lacked milk, and adolescents were emaciated and half starved.

Relief Measures

The Russians themselves were doing what they could, the better off assisting the poorer and the remainder pooling their scanty resources. There were five Russian Relief organizations at work, chief among them being the Russian Military Union or, as it is now known, the Union of Russian Army and Navy Ex-Service Men. This body kept going two soup kitchens and maintained a home where 150 were always lodged. It made advances to individuals to enable them to set up in business, acted as an employment bureau and ran a bakery, a kitchen garden and a shoemaker's shop.

But Russian efforts by themselves were totally inadequate to the situation, and, in June 1923, a Russian Refugee Relief Committee was formed. This body, before it was wound up in March 1925, received, mainly from foreign sources, and spent over $46,-000 on relief work. It ran two soup kitchens, where for 20 months between 500 and 800 were fed daily, it helped to finance a shelter where 60 men, women and children were accommodated, gave assistance in maternity cases and provided milk for delicate children. It repatriated 465 and assisted others to emigrate to Canada.

A particular responsibility was felt to be the boys of the two cadet schools left behind by Admiral Stark. These were housed in Jessfield Road under the supervision of their old teachers. Here they did all their own work and food costs were kept down to 25 cents a day. Even this for over 300 boys mounted up to $2,000 a month, but the money was found. Meanwhile it was impossible to arrange for their future—Shanghai had none to offer them—and attempts were made to find them a home elsewhere. The rich United States refused to take them but poor Serbia did not. With the French Consul-General and M. Grosbois, head of the French School, behind it a lottery was organized to raise the necessary funds for their transportation, and to Serbia the bulk of these cadets eventually went.

Orthodox Confraternity

To thinking people, however, something more than soup kitchens was needed if these unfortunate people were to be saved from the pit yawning at their feet. If misery, want and utter hopelessness was not to drive them down until they lost all self-respect and national pride and became submerged in China's teeming masses, they needed to be given moral support, helped to remember they were still members of a great nation, given evidence that they were members of a community. With this aim in view, the Russian Orthodox Confraternity was formed in February, 1923. The first objective was the creation of a communal feeling. Meetings and debates were held, speakers were sent out to address groups in different parts of the city, and thus a disorganized mob which had assembled in Shanghai from all parts of Russia, was welded into a Russian Community, membership of which gave the individual a sense of external support to aid him in his struggle against the forces threatening to drag him down.

Having done this, the Confraternity set itself to provide more tangible help. In October, 1923, with the aid of a grant from the American Red Cross it opened a dispensary where first-aid treatment was rendered and free medicines were supplied. Out of this grew a hospital, and three years later one of 10 beds was opened. The interest and encouragement of doctors and friends in the other foreign communities, financial assistance from the two foreign municipalities, the voluntary services of Russian doctors and the devotion of Russian nurses enabled it to be steadily enlarged. New premises were obtained which gave room for a maternity ward, a mental ward with 35 beds, was opened in connection with it, and to-day it has accommodation for 125 patients.

Schools were as urgently needed as the hospital. In their extremity some of the refugees had been driven to sending their children—babies, one might almost say, for some of them were only mites of three or four—to hawk cigarettes, matches, cheap toys and the like on the streets. An appeal for funds to care for these was readily responded to by the public, and in a house on Avenue Foch a school accommodating 25 children with full board was opened. Thus originated the School for Poor Russian Children, now the Russian Commercial School. By the end of 1923 it was housing 60 and in the years following steadily expanded. The French Municipal Council helped by providing a site for a new building, then the Rotary Club took up the task of raising a building fund—the Shanghai Movie Queen Contest was a notable incident in its drive for funds—and in 1933 the school moved into its present premises on Avenue Petain. Nearly 400 pupils now attend it, about half of them being boarders.

(To be continued)

本地俄裔社群的起源与未来

系列趣味文章之二，具有本地历史价值；难民问题如何考验上海的资源

下文将刊登专为《上海星期时报》撰写的五篇系列文章中的第二篇，内容涉及上海的俄裔社群——其起源、历史、组织及未来前景。

本篇特别探讨1923年因数千名赤贫的俄国难民涌入上海而产生的问题，并讲述俄国人如何组织成一个俄裔社群，以及为改善其境遇所做的工作。

对于任何城市而言，要应对像俄国难民抵沪所导致的成年人口如此大规模且突然的增长，本就是一件十分困难的事。而对上海来说，这尤其艰难。

首先，这些难民的责任并非由全市三百万居民共同承担，而是落在其中四万多外国人的肩上。其次，许多就业途径对新来者关闭。在欧洲城市，如果其他办法都行不通，他们本可以加入体力工业劳动或非技术劳工的行列。即使这类工作报酬不高，意味着在经济阶梯上的地位下降，也不会导致种族声望或民族自尊心的丧失。而在上海，这类工作由苦力从事，其工资远低于最卑微的难民所习惯的水平。难民只有融入中国苦力阶层，与他们同住同生活，才有望以此维持生存；而且，即便语言障碍能够克服，这也并非任何人所乐见的解决方案。

国联无所作为

1922年之后的几年里，上海和俄国人确实面临着一个非常棘手的问题——双方都有理由期望国际联盟帮助他们解决这一问题。该机构设立了一个由南森博士（Dr. Nansen）领导的委员会，专门处理战争难民问题，仅英国就为此项工作捐赠了15万英镑。1923年，向国联提交了一份关于远东状况的报告，同年12月，吉林爱尔兰长老会传教团的格里格博士（Dr. Grieg）被任命为南森委员会的中国代表。他将对局势进行全面调查，以寻求“中国俄国难民问题的最终解决方案”。

他的最终建议是遣返和移民，但这并没有起到太大帮助。很难指望难民回到等待他们的、落入红色敌人手中的命运中去；而没有资金支付交通费并确保获准进入心仪的国家，移民也是不可能的。由于难民本身几乎身无分文，而国联要么不愿、要么无法自行提供必要资金，最终的解决办法是让俄国人依靠上海外侨所能提供的帮助，自行谋求出路。

4000名赤贫俄国人

1923年从上海发给国联的一份报告有力地证明了援助需求的迫切性。报告称，当时在上海的7000多名俄国人中，超过一半完全赤贫，其余的人则靠担任职员、店员、司机、家仆、报贩和打零工勉强维持生计。他们住在最贫困地区的卫生条件恶劣的房屋里，甚至住在中国人房屋的单间里。他们没有浴室或蚊帐，家具和被褥寥寥无几。施粥处每天提供的一顿面包和汤是许多人唯一的食物来源，而大多数人的衣着也破旧不堪。儿童没有学校可上，婴儿缺乏牛奶，青少年则消瘦不堪，处于半饥饿状态。

救济措施

俄国人自身也在尽其所能，较富裕者帮助较贫困者，其他人则 pooling 他们微薄的资源。当时有五个俄国救济组织在开展活动，其中最主要的是俄国军人联合会，即如今所知的俄国陆海军退伍军人联合会。该机构维持着两个施粥处，并经营着一所收容所，常年收容150人。它向个人提供预付款以帮助他们创业，充当职业介绍所，并经营一家面包店、一个菜园和一家修鞋铺。

但仅靠俄国人的努力完全不足以应对局势，因此，1923年6月成立了俄国难民救济委员会。该机构在1925年3月解散之前，主要从国外来源接收并支出了超过46,000美元用于救济工作。它运营着两个施粥处，在20个月期间每天为500至800人提供食物；它资助了一所收容所，容纳60名男女老少；它为产妇提供援助，并为体弱儿童提供牛奶。它遣返了465人，并协助其他人移民加拿大。

人们感到有一项特殊的责任，那就是斯塔克海军上将（Admiral Stark）留下的两所军校的学生。这些学生住在极司菲尔路（Jessfield Road），由他们以前的老师监管。在这里，他们自己做所有的工作，食物成本控制在每天25美分。即便如此，300多名男孩每月的费用也高达2,000美元，但这笔钱还是筹措到了。与此同时，无法为他们的未来做出安排——上海无法为他们提供任何前途——因此试图在其他地方为他们寻找归宿。富有的美国拒绝接收他们，但贫穷的塞尔维亚却没有拒绝。在法国总领事和法国学校校长格罗斯布瓦先生（M. Grosbois）的支持下，组织了一次彩票活动以筹集必要的运输资金，最终大部分军校学生前往了塞尔维亚。

东正教兄弟会

然而，对于有识之士来说，如果要使这些不幸的人免于陷入脚下的深渊，仅靠施粥处是不够的。如果不希望贫困、匮乏和彻底的绝望使他们沉沦，直至失去所有的自尊和民族自豪感，并淹没在中国庞大的人群中，就需要给予他们道德支持，帮助他们铭记自己仍然是一个伟大民族的成员，并向他们证明他们是社群的一员。本着这一目标，俄国东正教兄弟会于1923年2月成立。首要目标是营造一种社群感。举行会议和辩论，派遣演讲者到城市不同地区向群体发表讲话，从而将从俄罗斯各地聚集到上海的这群乌合之众凝聚成一个俄裔社群，成为其中一员使个人获得了一种外部支持感，有助于他对抗那些试图将他拖垮的力量。

在完成这一任务后，兄弟会着手提供更实质性的帮助。1923年10月，在美国红十字会的拨款援助下，开设了一家诊疗所，提供急救治疗并免费供应药品。由此发展出一家医院，三年后开设了一家拥有10张床位的医院。其他外侨社群中医生的关注和鼓励、朋友的支持、两个外国市政当局的财政援助、俄国医生的志愿服务以及俄国护士的奉献精神，使得医院得以稳步扩大。获得了新的场所，增设了产科病房，并开设了拥有35张床位的精神科病房，如今它可容纳125名病人。

学校的需求与医院一样迫切。在极度困境中，一些难民被迫让他们的孩子——简直可以说是婴儿，因为其中一些只有三四岁大——在街头兜售香烟、火柴、廉价玩具等物品。公众对照顾这些儿童的筹款呼吁积极响应，在福煦路（Avenue Foch）的一所房屋里，开办了一所容纳25名儿童并提供全膳的学校。贫苦俄国儿童学校由此诞生，即如今的俄国商业学校。到1923年底，该校已收容60名学生，并在随后几年稳步扩张。法租界公董局通过提供新校舍用地予以帮助，随后扶轮社承担了筹集建筑基金的任务——上海电影皇后评选是其筹款活动中的一件 notable 事件——1933年，学校迁至贝当路（Avenue Petain）的现址。目前约有400名学生就读，其中约一半为寄宿生。

（待续）
